#9875. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

#9873. [$] Locking down hibernation for the winter

When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off. Unfortunately, the kernel does not have any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with, which is why lockdown, an optional kernel feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation. Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared a patch set that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.

#9872. Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions

Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave.

World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes.

Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus."

The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom "nature makes no leaps," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference.

Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time."

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action.

But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted.

Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions.

Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur.

"In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were.

"Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction."

Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements.

"The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken.

"Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces.

"We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case."

Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot retry an action after a surprise event.

"When an attempt fails because of something the robot could not see, such as an unexpected load, a current or a weak motor, the counterfactual world model lets it estimate which action would have worked in that same situation," he explained. "In our simulated tasks, choosing the action this way reaches the goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner that knows the true simulator but ignores the observed outcome. With two more attempts on the same event, success rises to 51 to 97 percent."

He also sees these models being useful for adapting to persistent fault, like a miscalibrated motor, and helping people understand failures.

"World models are trained to predict, and they are getting good at it," said Balestriero. "But a robot, a car or a drone acting in the real world is constantly surprised by things it could not see coming. After a surprise, the useful question is no longer what was expected, but what would have happened had it acted differently in that same situation. You need that answer to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, or to decide what to do on the next attempt, and prediction alone does not provide it."

The researchers initial attempts to address the issue involved adding a learned component to the world model that infers whatever hidden disturbance (e.g. the current in the boat scenario) affected the anticipated outcome. But that approach was too fragile.

"Trying to understand why led to the theory," explained Balestriero. "Learning the disturbance from ordinary data is not just hard, it is impossible in general: the hidden noise can be relabeled differently for each action without changing a single prediction, so the data cannot tell you which labeling is the right one. The missing piece has to come from outside the data. For physical systems, it comes from the fact that forces add and that their interaction builds up slowly in time. Once you accept that, the learned disturbance model becomes unnecessary: the gap between what happened and what was predicted already carries the information you need, and you carry it over to the other action."

Balestriero said that control engineers have been implementing corrections of this sort for decades, to tune hand-built models.

"What was missing was why the same correction is justified for learned world models that see the world through images, what can and cannot be recovered without paired data, and where it breaks," he said. "The paper answers these questions by connecting causal inference, control and world models. The title comes from Leibniz's law of continuity, natura non facit saltus, 'nature makes no leaps,' which is precisely the property that makes all of this work."

The researchers' paper was provided to The Register prior to its release on ArXiv. It is expected to be released this week. ®

#9871. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

#9869. Researchers pwn automakers’ Android apps to remotely unlock cars, honk horns

Pair of researchers chain WAF bypasses and default logins to command vehicles in Australia and the US

Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns.

Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US.

The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments."

Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai, Kia, Subaru, and many others.

In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses.

They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses.

This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app.

Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console.

The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. They then used Felix configuration manager to schedule a task that executed an inline Groovy script, giving them shell access to the identity servers.

The researchers then queried local admin API endpoints, allowing them to view or modify user account data. From there, they logged into car owners’ accounts, and gained the ability to issue the same commands as demonstrated in the Australian version.

According to Curry’s disclosure timeline, he and Shah approached the affected automakers in "early 2026," and the exploits were patched within two hours of receiving the report.

Although the automakers wished to remain anonymous, it didn’t take long for some petrolheads to speculate that the partially blurred car in Shah’s demo video was a Toyota, citing the shape of the wing mirror and the unlock sound it made.

Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. Asked wether the claims were accurate, a spokesperson for Toyota Motor Corporation neither confirmed nor denied them.

Curry said he and Shah chose to uphold the manufacturers’ requests to remain anonymous out of concern for infoseccers’ current workloads.

He said: "Obviously, they have asked not to be named, and while normally we would fight to actually include the company names, it's a busy time in the security world and I don't like the idea of them diverting resources because they are worried about something with this disclosure." ®

#9868. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9867. What's new in Node.js 27

Node.js 27 brings V8 15.6 with Iterator.zip, Iterator.zipKeyed, Math.sumPrecise, net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, and a 4 GB default heap limit.

On October 29, 2026, the Node.js team published v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0. If you have been using Node.js for a few years, that version string alone probably made you do a double take. Where is the usual October v27.0.0 Current release?

Node.js 27 is the first release to follow the new annual schedule. Under the old schedule, October brought a major release that reached end of life six months later without entering Long Term Support (LTS). October now starts a six-month Alpha phase, ahead of the 27.0.0 Current release in April 2027 and LTS promotion in October 2027.

Wait, an odd-numbered Node.js release becoming LTS?

Yes, the odd/even split is gone. Version numbers now match the calendar year (27 in 2027), with one major release per year, and every release becomes LTS. We covered the timeline and the reasons for the change in Node.js is changing its release schedule and version numbers. Because Node.js 27 is currently in its Alpha window, I will keep updating this article as new builds land on the way to April 2027.

In this first Alpha, V8 moves from 14.6 to 15.6, adding Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), and Math.sumPrecise(). There is a promises API for node:net, along with async-iterable TCP servers. The Virtual File System (node:vfs) is now unflagged, the Permission Model gains --allow-env, and HTTP and memory defaults change too.

We’ll start with the JavaScript and Node.js APIs you can use in everyday code, comparing them with the older approaches. Then we’ll cover runtime changes and what to check before upgrading.

Every code block with a file path in its title matches a runnable file in the companion repo lmammino/nodejs-27-examples on GitHub.

For example, we can format a list of products and total their prices:

If you want to experiment locally, check your current Node.js version before running the snippets below.

This is the part of the release I’m most excited about. I love seeing how far we can push streams, iterators, and generators. Our article on JavaScript async iterators should give you an idea of what I mean.

In What’s new in Node.js 26, we used Iterator.concat() to consume multiple iterables one after another. Node.js 27, through V8 15.6, lets us consume them side by side, pairing values at the same position.

Suppose you are checking a weather forecast against the temperatures recorded over the same four days. The predictions come from your model, while the actual values come from observations. To calculate each day’s error, you need to pair the values at the same position. Both sequences must cover the same days in the same order.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, if both sequences were arrays, you would typically use .map() with an index lookup:

That works well for arrays. But what if observations come from a generator, or your model returns an iterator of predictions? Index lookups won’t work on those inputs, and converting them to arrays means loading both sequences into memory first.

In Node.js 27, Iterator.zip() takes an iterable of iterables and returns a lazy iterator of pairs. We can calculate the errors with the same pipeline whether the inputs are arrays or iterators:

Each pair contains a prediction and its corresponding observation. A positive error means the day was warmer than predicted; a negative error means it was cooler. The pairing and mapping happen one item at a time. Only the final .toArray() collects the errors into an array so we can print them together.

Another common use is the dot product of two vectors: multiply matching components, then add the products. This operation appears in graphics, machine learning, and numerical computing:

Here we never collect the pairs or products into an intermediate array. We also use mode: 'strict' because a dot product requires vectors of equal length: silently ignoring extra components would hide an input error.

By default, Iterator.zip() uses { mode: 'shortest' }: it stops when the shortest input finishes and closes the remaining open iterators. For the forecast example, that means comparing only the days available in both sequences. Use { mode: 'strict' } if a missing prediction or observation should instead throw a TypeError. Or pass { mode: 'longest', padding: [null, 0] } to continue until the longest input finishes, using the corresponding padding value when an input runs out.

So far, our inputs have been arrays. But Iterator.zip() also works with iterators that have no end. Imagine a home with two power meters: one measures solar generation, and the other measures household consumption. Each meter gives us its current reading in watts whenever we poll it. Subtracting consumption from generation tells us whether the house has surplus power to export or needs to import power from the grid (assuming there is no battery).

We can wrap each meter in an endless generator. Here we simulate the readings with random values so the example runs without hardware:

Neither generator reads anything until we request a value from netPower. Each request polls both meters once and calculates the difference. Both input iterators can keep producing readings forever, but .take(5) limits this demo to five pairs. Collecting either input with [...solar] or .toArray() would never finish and would eventually exhaust memory.

These are synchronous, on-demand readings: the two meters are polled sequentially, close together, rather than at exactly the same instant. The loop takes five readings immediately; zip() does not add a polling interval. With real hardware, the callbacks would read the meters instead of generating random numbers.

Tuple arrays like [prediction, observation] are easy to read for two or three items, but once you have four or five parallel sources, positional destructuring gets easy to mix up.

Iterator.zipKeyed() accepts an object whose values are iterables. Each step yields an object with the same keys, so you can refer to values by name instead of position:

If an API returns each field as a separate array, like user IDs, names, and roles, Iterator.zipKeyed() lets you process them together as a lazy sequence of row objects. The arrays must describe the same records in the same order.

In Node.js 26, a common way to format a lazy iterator pipeline as a string was to call .toArray().join(', ') at the end. The final .toArray() allocated an array of strings that .join() consumed and discarded.

V8 15.6 adds two terminal helpers directly onto Iterator.prototype:

For join(), let’s return to our sensor readings. This time we only need one temperature sensor, and we want to format five readings as a comma-separated string. As before, we simulate the hardware so you can run the example locally:

.take(5) makes the endless source finite, .map() formats each reading, and .join() builds the string without collecting an intermediate array. These five readings are taken immediately, with no delay between them. Without .take(5), joining this endless iterator would never finish.

For includes(), imagine checking whether a commit message references a particular issue. String.prototype.matchAll() already returns an iterator, so we can extract the complete references and search them directly:

includes() stops as soon as it finds APP-142, without extracting the later reference. Matching complete references also avoids the false positive you would get from message.includes('APP-14'), which matches part of APP-142. The search consumes the iterator, so create a fresh one for another search.

The iterator helpers shown above work with synchronous iterators. Their .next() calls return results directly; these helpers do not await promises from async iterators. You cannot use the same chains on an async function* generator or a Node.js readable stream’s async iterator. Use for await...of or a library with async iterator helpers for those sources. Async iterator helpers are covered by a separate TC39 proposal and are not built into Node.js 27 as of v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0.

Beyond iterator helpers, V8 15.6 also brings a useful addition for numerical calculations: Math.sumPrecise(). To see why it matters, let’s look at a familiar floating-point surprise.

When you sum numbers with .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0), each addition rounds its intermediate result to the nearest representable 64-bit float. Over dozens or thousands of additions, those tiny rounding errors accumulate. Worse, if you add a small number (0.1) to a huge number (1e20) and later add -1e20, the 0.1 is lost completely during the first addition because a 64-bit float doesn’t have enough mantissa bits to hold both magnitudes at once.

In Node.js 27, V8 15.6 enables Math.sumPrecise() by default. It accepts any iterable of numbers, computes the sum using an internal high-precision accumulator, and rounds only once at the very end:

Math.sumPrecise() accepts any iterable, so it also works with the iterators from the previous section. You can pass the result of .map() directly into Math.sumPrecise() without calling .toArray() first:

When you still need integer cents or decimal libraries

Math.sumPrecise() avoids rounding after each addition. Its result is what you would get by adding the exact mathematical values of the input floating-point numbers, then rounding the total once to the nearest representable 64-bit float. But those inputs may already differ from the decimal values you intended:

As the MDN explanation points out, the literals 0.1 and 0.2 are stored as binary floating-point values slightly greater than their exact decimal counterparts. Adding those stored values and rounding once still produces 0.30000000000000004. The method cannot recover the intended decimal inputs.

For money calculations that require exact decimal arithmetic, use integer minor units (like cents) or a decimal library with explicit rounding rules. Math.sumPrecise() improves summation accuracy; it does not turn JavaScript numbers into decimal numbers.

The core node:net module gets iterator support too.

For years, node:fs, node:dns, node:stream, node:timers, and node:readline have all had .promises sub-modules. Yet node:net remained purely callback- and event-driven. If you wanted to spin up a TCP server on an ephemeral port in a test or connect a client socket using async/await, you had to wrap 'listening', 'connect', and 'error' events by hand.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, setting up a TCP server and client with async/await looked like this:

Node.js 27 introduces the experimental node:net/promises module with two helpers, listen() and connect(), and makes net.Server itself an async iterable.

Let’s try something fun and build a small TCP chat server. Each connected client can send a line of text, and the server forwards it to every other client, prefixed with the sender’s connection ID:

Then open two or three other terminals and run this command in each (with netcat installed):

Each terminal receives its connection ID, for example Connected as 127.0.0.1:54321. Type a message and press Enter. The other terminals receive a line such as 127.0.0.1:54321 > Hello everyone!. The server does not echo messages back to their sender. Press Ctrl+C in a client terminal to disconnect, or in the server terminal to close the chat and all active connections.

With three netcat clients connected, each terminal receives the other clients’ messages:

listen() resolves once the server is listening. The clients map tracks active sockets by their remote address and port, which distinguish connections to this server. These are connection labels, not permanent user identities: reconnecting can give a client a different port.

Inside each handler, readline turns the socket’s byte stream into lines. TCP chunks do not correspond to messages: a line may arrive in several chunks, or one chunk may contain several lines. Each completed line is broadcast to every other active socket. The finally block removes disconnected clients and closes their resources.

The outer connection loop starts each handleConnection(socket) call without awaiting it. That lets it accept the next client while earlier handlers wait for messages. Each handler still awaits its own incoming lines, so clients can remain connected and chat concurrently. The .catch() handles rejected handler promises; socket errors are handled separately, and server.maxConnections = 10 caps open connections for this demo.

The pitfall: awaiting each connection handler

This small change would break the chat’s concurrency:

handleConnection() stays active until its client disconnects. Awaiting it here means only the first client gets a handler and joins the clients map. Later connections can be accepted by the server, but the loop will not dispatch their handlers until that first client leaves. There is nobody else in the map to receive the first client’s messages!

The server iterator documentation warns that a slow consumer can buffer connections without bound. Set server.maxConnections explicitly and choose a limit appropriate to your workload, including when dispatching handlers concurrently.

The iterator yields TCP connections, not individual chat messages or application-level requests. Awaiting a handler can be appropriate for deliberate sequential processing, but a chat server needs overlapping connection handlers.

Testing code that reads configuration files often means mocking node:fs or creating temporary directories and cleaning them up afterward. Bundling assets or templates into an archive poses a related problem: how can your application read them through its usual node:fs calls?

The new node:vfs (Virtual File System) module was originally introduced behind --experimental-vfs, and in Node.js 27 it is unflagged and available out of the box (though still marked Experimental Stability 1 while the API settles).

With node:vfs, you can create an isolated, in-memory file system with vfs.create(), populate it using standard fs-style methods, and mount it so regular node:fs operations (and import / require()) can read from it directly. VirtualFileSystem also supports Explicit Resource Management (using), which unmounts it when execution leaves the block:

The using declaration tells JavaScript to call memoryFs[Symbol.dispose]() when execution leaves the block, including when an error is thrown. VirtualFileSystem implements that method to unmount itself. Declaring it with const would require us to call unmount() explicitly.

memoryFs.mount() mounts the virtual file system under a reserved namespace (path.join(os.devNull, 'vfs'), such as /dev/null/vfs/1 on POSIX), so a virtual mount can never accidentally shadow or overwrite real files on your disk. If you want to compare this with working on real files, check out our guide on reading and writing files in Node.js.

You can also use node:vfs through --vfs-load on the CLI without an experimental flag:

That command mounts the companion repo’s 04-vfs/bundle directory and runs its index.js, which prints Hello from the VFS bundle. You can also pass a ZIP archive; Node.js runs its package.json "main" or index.js entry point from the mounted archive. And if you use Single Executable Applications (SEA), vfsArchive is now mounted at layer 0 and automatically available inside Worker threads too.

There are changes across the standard library too, from temporary files to HTTP server defaults.

Until now, if you needed a temporary file in Node.js, your safest built-in option was fs.mkdtemp() to create a temporary directory, and then opening a file inside it. Creating a random filename yourself and calling fs.open() was error-prone and required a retry loop in case of collisions.

Node.js 27 adds APIs modeled on POSIX mkstemp(3): fs.mkstemp(), fs.mkstempSync(), and fsPromises.mkstemp(). It atomically generates a unique filename (appending six random characters to your prefix) and opens the file in a single step, returning both the path and the open FileHandle (or file descriptor fd):

The built-in fs.glob() (introduced in Node.js 22) was ported from JavaScript to native C++ in Node.js 27. The maintainers’ benchmarks show substantial speedups for some workloads, but gains vary by API and options, and one synchronous exclude-pattern workload regressed. Benchmark your own patterns before assuming a speedup.

As we covered in our guide to environment variables in Node.js, process.env is where most applications keep their most sensitive secrets (API keys, database URLs, signing tokens). It is also the very first place a compromised dependency looks when trying to exfiltrate credentials.

Node.js 27 adds --allow-env to the Permission Model (--permission). When --permission is enabled, every environment variable not explicitly matched by --allow-env is scrubbed at process startup before any JavaScript runs (except runtime variables like PATH, HOME, LANG, and NODE_OPTIONS, plus variables explicitly loaded via --env-file):

Node.js also scrubs disallowed variables from the underlying OS environment block and restricts access to /proc/self/environ on Linux. Native code loaded by Node.js sees the reduced environment too. This reduces accidental exposure; the Permission Model is not a sandbox for malicious code. You can remove a variable after reading it with process.permission.drop('env', 'VARIABLE_NAME'). Keep NODE_ENV explicitly if your application uses it, since it is not preserved by default.

The built-in node:test runner has three updates:

These three HTTP changes affect production web servers:

If you are curious why this change was made: it seems a bit weird on the surface, right? Why would Node.js remove the prototype from an otherwise ordinary object?

req.headers is a dictionary: the keys are header names chosen by whoever sent the request, and the values are whatever they sent. An ordinary JavaScript object is a poor fit for that kind of data, because it inherits properties from Object.prototype that have nothing to do with what you stored in it:

Our empty ordinary object already “has” a constructor, inherited from its prototype. __proto__ is even more surprising: Object.prototype defines an accessor with that name, so reading it returns the prototype, and assigning to it tries to change the prototype instead of storing a value. Both names are already lowercase, which matters here because Node.js lowercases incoming header names. A client can send a constructor or __proto__ header, and it arrives under exactly that key.

Notice that the example uses __proto__ in two different ways. { __proto__: null } is special object-literal syntax that creates the object with no prototype at all (Object.create(null) does the same thing, and the new Node.js code uses the literal form). The later headers['__proto__'] = ... is an ordinary assignment: with no inherited __proto__ setter to intercept it, it simply stores an own property, like any other key.

That’s the motivation in PR #62900, by Matteo Collina. Besides consistency with the *Distinct APIs, its commit message says the change “Fixes prototype pollution concerns where headers like __proto__ could be interpreted as prototype manipulation.” My reading is that the goal is clean dictionary semantics: a key exists in req.headers only if the request sent it.

The March 2026 security releases already included a real bug of this kind. CVE-2026-21710 was a denial-of-service flaw in req.headersDistinct, and it went like this:

Because the exception is thrown synchronously inside a property getter, an 'error' event listener can’t catch it. The fix initialized the headersDistinct and trailersDistinct objects with { __proto__: null }, which is the behavior PR #62900 later extended to headers and trailers. The advisory covers headersDistinct only, so it doesn’t mean req.headers had the same crash. The bug also stopped at crashing the process: a header couldn’t use it to modify Object.prototype globally. And a null-prototype object removes inherited-property hazards only where the headers are created. If you merge headers into an ordinary object, that target still has the inherited __proto__ accessor.

Node.js 27 also updates its engine and bundled dependencies. Most of the V8 details below come from Joyee Cheung’s Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha) on the Node.js blog, which is worth reading in full if you maintain performance-sensitive code or native tooling:

Default Heap Limit up to 4 GB on mid-sized machines: When --max-old-space-size is not specified, V8 now sets the default old-generation heap limit to half of physical memory (or container cgroup memory), clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB. Previously, machines with less than 15 GB of RAM were capped at 2 GB. On an 8 GB container or VM, the default old-generation limit therefore rises from 2 GB to 4 GB (and on a 6 GB machine, from 2 GB to 3 GB). These are old-generation limits, not limits on the process’s total memory use.

Buffer and ArrayBuffer memory affects garbage collection scheduling: Memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances is now included in V8’s global allocation limit. If your app allocates large off-heap buffers (for example, image processing or large file buffers), this affects when garbage collection is scheduled. The global allocation limit is distinct from the old-generation heap limit and does not impose a hard cap on the process’s total memory.

Slightly more memory per worker and per native object: Each V8 isolate (the main thread and every worker thread) uses about 180 KB more for property lookup caches, and every JavaScript object that wraps a native resource (a socket, file handle, stream, hash, or blob) may use about 16 bytes more on the heap and about 50 bytes more outside it. That’s negligible for most apps, but it adds up if you spawn many workers or hold many open sockets.

Fewer hard crashes on fatal errors: More fatal V8 errors now go through Node.js’s fatal error handling before aborting, so --report-on-fatalerror can produce a diagnostic report in cases that previously aborted without one. Some extreme inputs (overly long template literals, classes with too many elements, a regexp too large to compile) now throw a RangeError instead of crashing the process. The V8 post is explicit that this isn’t guaranteed, so don’t build program logic around it.

These numbers come from V8’s own benchmarks, and the impact varies with platform, workload, and build configuration. Measure your application before counting on a speedup.

OpenSSL 4.1.0, Undici 8.12, SQLite 3.54, and npm 12.1.0: Node.js 27 upgrades its bundled cryptography to OpenSSL 4.1.0, strips out all legacy OpenSSL 1.x compatibility shims and engine APIs, bumps npm to 12.1.0, and updates NODE_MODULE_VERSION to 153.

The Alpha window gives you time to check for breaking changes before the stable release. Most applications won’t encounter all of these, but check your code and dependencies for the following changes.

As we saw in the HTTP section, the header dictionaries no longer have a prototype. Normal property access (req.headers['content-type']), destructuring, and Object.keys() work as before. What breaks is calling methods inherited from Object.prototype: req.headers.hasOwnProperty('authorization') now throws a TypeError (and calling a method looked up on a dictionary of external data was never a good idea anyway).

Replace it with Object.hasOwn(req.headers, 'authorization'), which doesn’t rely on the object’s prototype and works on both Node.js 26 and 27. Please don’t “fix” this by restoring Object.prototype on the headers object. The in operator still works on null-prototype objects, but the updated Node.js docs advise against using it here, and Object.hasOwn() expresses the own-property check you actually mean.

This runnable example shows both the failure and the fix. Keep in mind that checking for a header’s presence does not authenticate its value:

If you run multiple Node.js processes on a 6 GB or 8 GB machine and relied on the old implicit 2 GB heap cap to keep them from starving each other, pass --max-old-space-size=2048 explicitly. Similarly, if your application holds hundreds of megabytes of Buffer data in memory alongside a large JS heap, be aware that Buffer allocations now influence V8’s global allocation limit and garbage collection scheduling.

Most V8 changes are invisible, but a few can break code that depends on exact results:

The V8 changes post lists more edge cases, including fractional getTimezoneOffset() values for historical dates and stricter take()/drop() limits on iterators.

When testing your project or library against Node.js 27:

For production, the release date matters. For library authors and local experiments, there is already code to try:

If you want to install the Alpha side by side with your stable LTS runtime without messing up your system setup, check out our guide on 5 ways to install Node.js using version managers like fnm or nvm.

Want to write modern, production-ready Node.js?

Our book Node.js Design Patterns covers streams, iterators, async control flow, modules, and scalable architectures. The runtime changes each year; these patterns help you design applications across releases.

Node.js 27 starts the annual release schedule, with every major version going on to LTS. Its first Alpha includes V8 15.6, node:net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, fs.mkstemp(), and --allow-env.

I’d start by trying Iterator.zipKeyed() and Iterator.prototype.join() in a data-transformation script. They let you process parallel collections lazily without collecting intermediate arrays.

For the full list of commits and low-level details, check out the official Node.js 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 release notes and the companion post on Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha).

Thanks to the Node.js releasers, V8 maintainers, and contributors who worked on this first Alpha and the new release schedule.

Node.js 27 is the first version under the new Node.js release schedule. Instead of two major releases per year, Node.js now ships one major release every April, preceded by a six-month Alpha testing phase starting in October.

Yes. Under the new release schedule, the old odd/even rule is gone and every yearly major release becomes LTS. Node.js 27 will enter Current in April 2027, move to LTS in October 2027, and be supported until April 2030.

Thanks to V8 15.6, Node.js 27 ships Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), Math.sumPrecise(), and Intl.Locale.prototype.variants enabled by default.

When --max-old-space-size is not set, V8 now defaults to half of physical memory clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB (meaning an 8 GB machine gets a 4 GB heap instead of 2 GB). Additionally, memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances now counts toward V8’s global allocation limit, affecting when garbage collection runs.

If you are reading this before April 2027, keep production workloads on an LTS release. Node.js 27 is still in its Alpha testing phase during that period, intended for library authors, CI pipelines, and experimentation. It is scheduled to enter Current in April 2027 and LTS in October 2027. Once a stable release is available, evaluate it against your application’s support requirements.

#9866. Amutable Foundations: A Technical Overview

Posted Nov 7, 2026 9:43 UTC (Sat) by alspnost (guest, #2763) [Link] (17 responses)

Quoting from the article: > Package-based OSes generally provide the user with a large number of regularly updated software packages (many thousands) with complex dependencies, which are composed into a working OS on the final machine it is deployed on. Installations in this style tend to vary greatly from system to system. Even with an identical selection of packages for the target system, the installation/update order, the stateful update logic and the file system data structures generally mean that the bytes that hit the disk on each machine are always different. This is called drift. > Systems put together this way are hence not reproducible, not predictable, and hard to compare and analyze which is essential for tracking down security issues. The second paragraph does not logically follow from the first paragraph. It is just a complete non-sequitur, but the word "hence" suggests otherwise. Systems put together this way can be reproducible, predictable, easy to compare and analyze. Side note: with ASLR, in-memory layout is not predictable, but only very few people complain about that and image-based OS don't make ASLR predictable either. There also is little conceptual difference between a flattened view of layered file system images for an image-based OS or a pre-flattened file system image for a package-based OS, just the time of flattening differs. One could even make a case that creating a flattened view of multiple file system layers at runtime is less reproducible than having a pre-flattened file system which is identical on every boot (at least in the read-only case). OTOH, maybe the Amutable people really have a hard time comparing and analyzing systems with package-based OSes. In that case, maybe their own solution is the only one they can easily work with, and hey... it is valid to create a system they can understand. That's the beauty of FOSS. I just wish they wouldn't bash choices different from their own.

By the time you start an upgrade and by the time it's actually done globally, there very well could have been a package update that came in at the end which the beginning ones did not receive. Many times, it's immaterial, yes -- distributions have done a great job at versioning and keeping non-breaking changes out of versioned releases, but it's a variance nonetheless. Not only packages, but even config changes within a fleets config management system can flow changes into it that the first round didn't, as changes get picked up. Often we don't have the convenience of downtime when managing baremetal systems, which something like Kubernetes abstracted away, but something still has to run baremetal. Amutable's core idea itself is not new, image-based and immutable cores have been around for a long time. What I find most interesting about their approach is the comprehensive approach they are taking with it, from offering a control plane and verification across the entire stack. I've seen these ideas employed in production individually, but am interested to see where they take it when it's coming entirely from the ground up.

Amutable's core idea itself is not new, image-based and immutable cores have been around for a long time. What I find most interesting about their approach is the comprehensive approach they are taking with it, from offering a control plane and verification across the entire stack. I've seen these ideas employed in production individually, but am interested to see where they take it when it's coming entirely from the ground up.

That said, if you have a configuration and package management which is idempotent, the suffering is not too bad. Debian with Saltstack is one such combination, but others exist as well. It helps to think of an image as a giant package where you have to update everything at once. Suddenly, the magic of images disappears. Additionally, there is no difference between a file system image and an archive. Case in point: The original Microsoft Word .doc files are more or less FAT file systems in a file. Another case in point: initramfs is a file system image which happens to use the cpio archive format as file system.

Additionally, there is no difference between a file system image and an archive. Case in point: The original Microsoft Word .doc files are more or less FAT file systems in a file. Another case in point: initramfs is a file system image which happens to use the cpio archive format as file system.

Now, of course, image-based solutions themselves aren't without their caveats either. You can't easily just pick any host in the fleet and then hand-modify it for the purposes of testing "just this one thing" while facing production traffic in a production environment. Which yes is a bad practice, but sometimes in an outage all-hands-on-deck scenario, having that flexibility is what saves hours of downtime. Image-based solutions, you have to run a whole CI to spit out a new image with your bumped version, then deploy it. Compared with SaltStack, you can run the state everywhere or even cmd.run it if the urgency calls for it and the change is small enough. But I think those are solvable problems and I think there's a middle-ground to be achieved there. For now, we remain primarily a SaltStack + package management fleet, but I am interested to see more ideas in this field when it comes to addressing systems management at this scale.

Image-based solutions, you have to run a whole CI to spit out a new image with your bumped version, then deploy it

I suppose that's why Amutable has these sysext/confext overlays. Just build an image with the package(s) you want to replace and boot the node with it on top.

Debuggability requirements tell me that there should be a way to do this without rebooting. I need a way to actually interact with a misbehaving system.

There are ways around this. For example, /etc can be made read-write, it's just not persistent across reboots. It's more of a pain if you want to install new packages, but in our case we have docker installed so plugins can be added. In that case you can build a docker image with the software you want, and then run the image with sufficient permissions to use the software in the way you want. Image based distributions mostly offer: (a) reboot goes back to known state each time, (b) updates cost fixed amount of time no matter the changes (reboot), (c) you know every system is running the same bits as you tested in your test environment. Amutable appears to offer this plus a whole signing mechanism to prove it's not tampered with, but that's not relevant in our case.

So hosts have to be updated at different times and subsequently inevitably see different package repositories during time-of-update. This in turn means that different hosts go through different upgrade paths now; and even if this is mostly not relevant for a well-managed stable distro, it is not really reproducible anymore. With image-based approaches you don’t have this problem; there are only two possible system states now: image X before update, and image Y after update – no matter if you have five or five hundreds of hosts, no matter if some hosts have been setup yesterday or last year. This is just tremendously more well-defined. I mean, for most operators this is not super relevant, because usually nothing happens; and most deployments are in such a bad shape that this is really not a concern for them. On the other hand, drift like this can be relevant IRL. I know, for example, that my previous employee got bitten by that once: Quite some years ago, something in some default configuration changed on Ubuntu – hosts that were older than X retained an old config, whereas newer setups had another default variant (no dist-upgrade mind you!), which caused some subtle but annoying reliability issues. For them, the solution also was to go image based – they already had a canary system in place to test updates and stuff; so instead of going apt on each system, they just took a snapshot from the canary and redeployed it everywhere every time. (There was an exception for critical security patches; those were installed immediately – any potential drift would be eliminated during the next regular snapshot deployment anyways.)

That's only because most classic distro update mechanisms lack version locking and instead always go to the latest package versions available in the repo. There is no need to go full image based, if you want to avoid that. The easiest and practical way to avoid this is to mirror the repository and not update it until all machines have received the update. I know that this doesn't make it fully reproducible, but it solves the "inevitably see different package repositories" part.

The easiest and practical way to avoid this is to mirror the repository and not update it until all machines have received the update. I know that this doesn't make it fully reproducible, but it solves the "inevitably see different package repositories" part.

That is quite obviously not true. Of course you can have multiple lock lists floating around at the same time in your corporate network. Lock lists = client side built "images".

This is a valid approach, especially given that it also has other advantages (clear audit trail of what packages changed when for example), but it is also tremendous maintenance overhead and only solves parts of the problem (e.g. this would not have helped against the problem of old installations vs new installations). And you can probably find a workaround for this problem too. Then you will discover another problem, and you can certainly find some bandaid for that as well. But... you could also just choose the architecturally sound approach here and go image-based. Whether it has to be OCI images, or disk images, or virtual machine images, or tar archives, or reference-based images via SHA2-manifests, or... that's a totally different question. But taking a seed and replicating that is always better and simpler than having a fleet of distinct systems, and then trying to come up with lots of bandaids to maybe hopefully eliminate all potential mutations to maybe hopefully ensure all the systems maybe hopefully are guaranteed to maybe hopefully evolve in exactly the same way. I mean, if people don't wanna go image-based for whatever reason that's fine – there are hundreds of different setups for hundreds of different use-cases; but if you want to have a fleet of identical systems, some approaches are more robust and easier to manage than others.

We have used this with (old) Redhat, Fedora Core, Ubuntu, Debian, Devuan, and back to Debian. Our Slackware days predate the controlled local mirror but I seem to recall we were using physical CDs to keep boxes in sync back then. We roll out updates from the local mirror to regression test nodes before deploying them to the live nodes.

We roll out updates from the local mirror to regression test nodes before deploying them to the live nodes.

Concur. Even with base image + app overlay based fleet management, you will never have uniform systems. Fleet diversity will scale at least logarithmically with size of fleet. You need to be able to live with diversity, because you're never going to have just 1 image deployed.

You need to be able to live with diversity, because you're never going to have just 1 image deployed.

As a sysadmin who manages fleets, I don't agree that reproducible system installation and update in package based systems is impossible. I have been doing it via xCAT (install) and SaltStack (update/manage) for a long time. You don't need these exact tools, but they are useful to us due to size of our fleets here. If you want extremely strict, SaltStack even has CF-Engine like drift-protection features yet I don't use them, because a system you don't touch doesn't drift.

Given a fixed state, any update set applied by apt and rpm are always deterministic. This is why they are so complex. Even so, this state can be the beginning and you can be bootstrapping a new image for yourself (I also did some distro development for some time).

Image based systems may have their advantages, but smearing other alternative to just strengthen one's position leaves a bad taste in my mouth, to be honest.

I've always wondered how much one can trust a factory reset. Let's put a real case: I had my phone hacked by a nation state some weeks ago. Their spies held it physically for several hours, and they had the PIN. Of course, after that, I don't trust that phone at all. Why would I trust the "factory reset" that comes with Android? I expect they could also tamper the image with which it is reset. At this point, the whole phone is a brick, IMO, and so I bought a new one.

I am unsure if AOS does it like this, but what Lennart has always been working towards is that the UEFI verifies the kernel (UKI) using the public key, which then verifies the /usr/ partition (which is read-only), which then loads the rest. "the rest" here would be the factory reset part, which is the only really modifiable part (also EFI variables get reset).

So say the nation state enrolled some kinda public key into the mutable part of the system (/var/ or possibly /etc/ but it sounds like it is also read-only) so that the system now also loads some of their system extensions or so, a factory reset would basically wipe those keys (and the extensions). /usr/ can't be enrolled, since that is pinned by the verity root hash and changes in the data would cause errors during reading by the kernel and the UKI is "pinned" by you (or I guess in the case of Amutable them) signing new UKIs. This is assuming you can prevent the nation state from enrolling their keys in your UEFI. But even if they did enroll their own keys in the UEFI the PCR values would be different, resulting in the mutable LUKS partitions not being automatically unlocked, so your mutable data is still inaccessible.

So as long as the cryptography implementations are sound and not bypassed by some 0-days it should be sound for the most part. Unless they are able to get below the bootloader it should be fine (but at that point they don't even need your PIN).

Do tell me if I maybe missed some attack vector which could possibly still exploit something.

Signed bootloaders won't save you if they control that.

#9865. Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets

Wiz researchers uncovered the secret-stealing supply-chain attack

Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship.

Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments.

“Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions.

Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries.

Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles.

The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote.

This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account.

Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store.

The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments.

Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data.

The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data.

While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity.

Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued.

Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses.

“For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®
