#9864. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9863. 'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

The malware's focus on AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook to expose a forest of AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint.

A novel infostealer that specifically targets AI applications and development tools is changing the narrative on illicit data monetization, opening up fresh revenue streams through extortion and other abuses of the stolen data.

Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things, they said in a recent report. It targets Windows-based machines and the browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications running on them — among other apps and services — with data theft.

However, Aokigahara is notable in that it has a particular focus on emerging AI-driven assets, collecting authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools, according to Check Point. This sets it apart from many of the infostealers currently active in the wild.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

"This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software," according to Check Point.

The AI data offers unique opportunities for threat actors to benefit financially from the stealer's activities by using credentials or session tokens to "enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts," according to the report.

The malicious activity can also extend to developer and cloud environments, and thus threaten enterprises. Indeed, threat actors have already demonstrated how they use stolen credentials for GitHub accounts, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files to infiltrate cloud environments of enterprise targets.

This may also pave the way for extortion of organizations by holding stolen data for ransom, according to Check Point.

"Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services," according to the post. "If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment."

Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of security firm Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that "stolen AI credentials can yield a heavy harvest for an attacker. A paid AI subscription is a resellable asset, and the conversation history behind it is often full of proprietary code, which means these stolen sessions now carry extortion value alongside their resale value."

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Other targeted data the malware looks for are developer and cloud credentials, including Git access data, SSH keys, and configuration files for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This data is valuable to give attackers access to private code repositories or cloud resources if the stolen credentials remain valid and have sufficient permissions, according to Check Point.

Indeed, "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring," Calderone observes, and some of those keys ultimately could give attackers access to the kingdom.

"The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run," he says.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

Aokigahara also has built-in anti-detection mechanisms. It checks for analysis environments such as virtual machines and sandboxes, and packages stolen data into zip archives and then encrypts it before sending it to attacker-controlled servers.

Aokigahara's targeting of AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook, potentially exposing AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint. The theft of this data then opens new pathways for financial gain for attackers and thus may provide an incentive for others to do the same, according to Check Point.

This means that defenders should start treating AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, with protections comparable to those applied to cloud credentials and developer keys. To that end, security teams should hunt for AI-session theft by investigating suspicious access to local application storage and authentication-related files belonging to AI assistants, coding agents, and developer IDEs.

Organizations also should more closely protect developer and cloud credentials by reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets on endpoints, using managed identity and short-lived credentials where feasible, and restricting access to cloud resources and source-code repositories.

Further, organizations can protect assets across exposed apps and tools by revoking exposed sessions and rotating secrets. If an endpoint is suspected of compromise, according to Check Point, they should assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens, not just browser passwords.

#9862. unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world

Co-founder of Assetnote, security researcher.

I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform.

Having looked at platforms like this before (previous works), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker".

When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet.

The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made.

Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au:

Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au. What else existed under this domain?

Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story.

One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it?

Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in.

I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do.

Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle.

For example, we could look up user accounts by email address:

But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that.

In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites.

Fortunately, there was an API that let you do exactly that:

Now, how do we send commands to any car we want? Surely this admin tool would let us do that? Unfortunately, no. It let us provision features to a car, add ourselves to a user's account as a secondary user, and even generate remote access codes. But for all that functionality, none of it actually got us remote control of a vehicle.

Sam and I then spent two weeks digging into how the automaker manages their central identity system: the software they use, the way commands are issued, and how consumers authenticate.

When a user goes through the authentication flow for the automaker's mobile app, requests are made to login.redacted-identity.com.au, and after going through an MFA flow, a consumer auth token is finally issued. This auth token is then used for subsequent requests to api.redacted-telematics.com.au (both REST APIs and GraphQL). Once you have that auth token, it's pretty much game over. You can control a user's car (remote unlock/lock, horns, engine, etc).

So if we could mint a token for any user, we'd finally be able to control anyone's connected car. This is the angle we went for.

The automaker is a heavy user of ForgeRock's identity software (OpenAM/OpenIDM). This is the cornerstone of their authentication mechanisms. Pulling the subdomains for *.redacted-identity.com.au, we quickly found their OpenIDM instance at openidm.redacted-identity.com.au. This is the system that manages every identity registered on the automaker's connected car platform.

This all clicked together when we were combing through the JavaScript files under *.redacted-telematics.com.au and we came across an absolutely cursed vendor JavaScript bundle that embedded admin credentials for OpenIDM 😱:

Even though these admin credentials were meant to be for their staging environment, given the hygiene we'd seen so far, we were pretty sure they'd work in production too.

Looking closer at OpenIDM, we couldn't tell whether the automaker knew how fragile it was. One thing was obvious though: they'd invested heavily in WAF rules to block access to the sensitive APIs that ForgeRock typically lets you call via /openidm/*.

Even with the origin IP, any request to /openidm/ came straight back as an Nginx WAF block. Someone had put real effort into hardening these assets (despite them being externally accessible).

Fair enough, and we respect the hardening. But that much WAF investment usually means bandaids over something known to be bad. They probably understood how bad it was to have this asset exposed at all, and some business case kept it there anyway.

I'm not sure a WAF rule has ever stopped us when we're motivated enough, so we invested days into finding a way out of these protections, using our trusty path traversal tricks. How hard could it be?

Validating the admin credentials we found inside the JavaScript bundle was not that tough. The Australian OpenIDM instance had a few paths whitelisted like /XUI/ and /UI/, and path traversal characters were not blocked, so something as simple as /XUI/..%2fopenidm/endpoint seemed to at least partially work:

But it can never be as simple as that, right? The path traversal still didn't get us to the endpoints under /openidm/, thanks to quirks in how OpenIDM handles routing. Every endpoint would error out like so:

In OpenIDM's world, there were no servlets (or resources) registered against paths that included the path traversal within them. So it would just error out, even though it issued us an admin JWT.

We were incredibly annoyed by this. A simple quirk in routing mechanisms (probably not even designed as a security consideration) was blocking the full attack chain from working. We sat frustrated for a few days, and we thought that the path traversal angle just wasn't going to work. We did find a few other endpoints (user upload, for example) that looked like they might work, but we hit another quirk, a servlet path check, that prevented us from using them meaningfully.

All of this made us ask a different question: why expose these OpenIDM instances externally at all? Surely there had to be some legitimate use case for these assets to be exposed on the internet? We went back to the different JavaScript bundles we had collected from their assets and searched them for communications to OpenIDM. We turned to the decompiled Android application and found the following:

These were clearly endpoints within their OpenIDM asset that were contactable from the Android app. So, maybe these were accessible without the WAF getting in the way?

What other custom endpoints existed? With some very light brute forcing and guessing, we quickly found a getUser endpoint. Guessing at parameters, we found it accepted mail, guid, and phone. Combined with our admin credentials, what did this really let us do?

The response came back with the password hash, PIN code hash, mobile push tokens, and PII including mobile numbers and full names. There was no WAF block on this endpoint, so no path traversal was needed and the correct servlet responded.

Don't get me wrong, this was already pretty impactful. But the passwords were hashed with PBKDF2-SHA512, and needing time on a hash cracking rig for every unlock, with no guarantee of success, felt a bit lacklustre.

Back to the drawing board. How could we access the /openidm/managed/user servlet with our path traversal, and still have the path be recognised by OpenIDM? We grabbed the OpenIDM source closest to the version we were testing against and let GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra spend a good six hours on it.

It succeeded. Even though Sam and I had both spent time trying to manually bypass this juvenile restriction ourselves, we hadn't tried every possible combination.

When Sam and I tried /XUI%2f..%2fopenidm/, we got a hard 403, and being human, we assumed that applied to every prefix. What GPT 5.6 found was that /static%2f..%2fopenidm/ wasn't covered by the WAF at all, and it gave us the OpenIDM APIs without the servlet confusion issue.

With this bypass, taking over an account became trivial. We could PATCH a new password for any user profile:

OK, so we could overwrite the password for any user. But what about multi-factor authentication?

Well, the automaker's Australian environment had one more misconfiguration: the multi-factor step could be skipped entirely. First, we requested an authentication token from login.redacted-identity.com.au with a Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, which returned a clean id_token we could swap for something usable in the consumer app:

We took that and moved on to step two, exchanging the first token for a session:

Lastly, we performed the token exchange for a mobile app access token:

It's super convoluted, I know. OAuth is annoyingly hard sometimes. But these steps let us bypass multi-factor authentication for any user of the automaker's connected car app.

At this point, we were so damn close to unlocking any of the automaker's cars in Australia. All that was left was issuing the command API requests with the app token we could now mint for anyone.

We obviously did all of this on cars we explicitly owned or had permission to interact with.

But let's take a step back and think about what we achieved here. We could send commands to any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, across both of their brands, by only knowing the number plate of the vehicle. The final chain looked like this:

At 12AM, when the full chain finally came together, I took a short video of the script in action. It's not polished, but it still felt magical seeing it all work. I definitely live for hard challenges like these.

You might be wondering: Shubs, you said any of their cars in the world. This only covers Australia. What gives?

There's a much more complex chain that Sam and I worked on together, which he's published on his blog here. It required a lot more work than the steps we took for Australia, as the automaker had spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments.

At the end of the day, with both writeups combined, we could send remote commands such as unlocking and turning the engines on, for any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

#9861. Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills

Nathan Hamiel outlines potential SecOps horror in the AI midst, as core technical capabilities go the way of reading an atlas or remembering phone numbers.

Black Hat India — Bengaluru — The use of AI as a tool to enhance cybersecurity operations is emerging as a double-edged knife for security professionals. While it can make them more capable, it could also spell the demise of the very skills they need to use it effectively.

That's the concern of Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, who has made a case for how evolving technology can erode technical skills since well before the generative AI boom. Now, that concern is getting much louder.

Speaking to Dark Reading recently, he says he began noticing the problem around 2005 and 2006, when he encountered cybersecurity professionals who lacked a firm grasp of the fundamentals of their work. At that time, he warned about the dangers of relying too heavily on various types of technical tools, declaring to cybersecurity professionals that "your tools are killing you," and warning that practitioners are moving away from being "hands-on" operators who investigate problems directly, and toward "hands-off" monitors who oversee results presented through tools, interfaces, and dashboards.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

It's a shift that's being exacerbated now by AI-driven automation, he says, and organizations need to move quickly to optimize the use of AI without the expense of cybersecurity skill-building.

While automation can simplify complex tasks and allow professionals to accomplish more, it can also distance them from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a solid understanding of the fundamentals, practitioners may struggle to recognize when a tool produces an incorrect result or when its findings require further investigation, Hamiel says.

"We need to keep these skills and not let them degrade because those skills are important to making the tools work in the best way possible," he tells Dark Reading from this week's Black Hat India conference, where he's giving a keynote entitled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems."

"What AI adds to somebody with knowledge and experience is some additional capabilities," Hamiel elaborates. "A domain expert wielding AI is going to be able to gain benefits from using that tool that a novice with no domain experience isn't going to be able to get."

This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into cybersecurity workflows. It also raises questions about how the industry will develop its next generation of experts if automation removes some of the hands-on tasks that junior professionals traditionally learn.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

The current discussion around AI often falls into extremes, Hamiel says. Some predict that the technology can go a long way toward solving major problems facing not only cybersecurity but also humanity, while others warn that it will bring the industry — and some even the world — to an end.

"You have the doomers," he says, "and you have people who say this is a big nothingburger. The truth is somewhere in the middle."

For Hamiel, understanding AI's impact requires separating what the technology can demonstrate in a controlled environment from what it can reliably accomplish in the real world. Impressive capabilities do not necessarily translate into the wholesale replacement of jobs or the disappearance of entire industries, he says.

The same distinction applies to cybersecurity, Hamiel says. Although AI can help identify vulnerabilities, generate code and support security investigations, those capabilities do not mean that the complex problems facing security teams have suddenly become easy to solve.

In fact, some recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity — such as OpenAI models autonomously hacking the Hugging Face framework, among others — may reveal a more familiar and persistent cybersecurity problem: organizations failing to address basic security weaknesses.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

"If you read some of the incident reports, these are organizations that weren't exercising basic security hygiene," Hamiel says.

In these cases, he argues, the weaknesses were already there, waiting to be discovered. "This wasn't just low-hanging fruit; this was fruit lying on the ground where anybody who looked for it would have found it," he says.

Rather than signaling an impending cybersecurity apocalypse, such incidents could prompt what Hamiel calls a "cybersecurity correction."

"It's not that there is this huge apocalypse happening; it's that many people weren't doing the right thing for a very long time," he explains.

In other words, AI may make it easier to discover and exploit existing weaknesses, exposing the consequences of inadequate security practices. The challenge for organizations is not simply to adopt new tools but to address the underlying problems those tools bring to light.

Indeed, the potential erosion of technical skills is not a problem that began with generative AI. Hamiel sees it as part of a longer trend in which technology increasingly mediates the relationship between professionals and the problems they are responsible for solving.

Hamiel's concern reflects what is often called the irony of automation: As systems take on more responsibility, the humans overseeing them can lose opportunities to practice the skills needed when those systems fail.

The consequences could extend beyond the skills of today's practitioners to the way the cybersecurity industry develops future experts, he says, especially in how lower-level work that AI can eliminate helps helping junior professionals learn.

Tasks that might appear repetitive or straightforward can provide essential experience, allowing new practitioners to understand how systems work before progressing to more complex investigations. "If you automate that, there isn't room for them to learn," Hamiel warns.

This creates a potential long-term problem for employers. AI may allow teams to complete certain tasks more efficiently today, but organizations still need experienced professionals who can investigate unfamiliar problems, evaluate automated findings, and respond when systems behave unexpectedly.

For cybersecurity pros to use generative AI effectively, then, it's simply a matter of applying it to tasks where it offers meaningful benefits while remaining aware of the skills that might be weakened if pros rely too much on these tools to do their jobs effectively.

"The goal here is to maximize the benefits and minimize the drawbacks," Hamiel says, something that is true for the use of any technology. "That's the framing that should be placed around this," he says.

Thus, the only way that organizations can adopt AI without losing essential cybersecurity expertise is to "apply them to the right types of activities," he says.

For cybersecurity pros, this means using generative AI for tasks such as threat hunting and threat intelligence, where preliminary analysis can help professionals work through information more efficiently, Hamiel notes. AI-powered penetration-testing tools are another area of promising development, extending beyond traditional vulnerability scanning to perform more complex tasks, he says.

Ultimately, the question is not whether AI will change cybersecurity, Hamiel says. That genie is most certainly already out of that bottle. Ultimately, the real challenge is ensuring that the industry does not become so dependent on increasingly capable tools that it loses the human expertise required to use them effectively, he says.

"Skills and expertise make your AI use more effective," Hamiel concludes. "If you have two professionals, and both use AI, the one with more knowledge of the task is going to make better use of the AI."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9860. France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns

The 'first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory'

France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.”

The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4).

The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers.

This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers.

The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers.

“The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.”

Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons.

First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says.

It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.”

In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C).

Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America.

The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.”

This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador.

However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

#9859. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9858. SBOMs Alone Can't Reveal the Scope of a Supply Chain Attack

A recent Shai-Hulud attack shows defenders need real-time visibility into production code and affected services to respond to supply chain compromises.

ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — Depending on a software bill of materials (SBOM) to determine what happens when a malicious package slips past security checks can leave defenders struggling to establish what code actually executed, which systems it touched, and how far the compromise spread.

In a session at the ISC2 Security Congress 2026 this week, Atlassian product security manager Deepam Kanjani used a real-world compromise involving the Shai-Hulud worm to highlight incident response challenges, including gaps in runtime visibility, transitive dependency ownership, and attacker attribution.

In the session, Kanjani said he had altered all identifying details, figures, and the sequence of events to protect confidentiality, though his first-person, war-room narrative of underlying attack techniques, technical behaviors, and challenges was based on real events at a large-scale software-as-a-service (SaaS) environment.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

Kanjani described the incident as involving a package that appeared legitimate, with a matching SHA hash, more than 3,400 GitHub stars, and a repository that looked credible to the company's security tooling. But hidden three layers deep in the package was a malicious transitive dependency named shai-hulud, after the giant sandworms in the Dune movie series. Because it was not a direct dependency, it did not surface in a top-level dependency audit.

The first inkling that something was wrong came when a behavioral scanner flagged the package as running something it shouldn't have been running. Incident responders initially dismissed the alert as a likely false positive because the hash matched and there was no other obvious indication of the package being malicious.

Additionally, the SBOM reported the environment as clean when the security team consulted it. What they did not realize at the time was that the SBOM was two development sprints out of date, Kanjani said.

As the response unfolded, the team could not say with confidence which services used the package. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided initial clues but could not establish which services were affected or how far the compromise had spread. Responders needed runtime evidence to determine what code had actually executed and what it could access.

Without that runtime telemetry, they had to correlate logs manually across more than 400 services, leaving them without a reliable picture of the compromise's potential reach. An initial Slack message from the incident response handler to enterprise stakeholders made matters worse by being too vague and prompting a set of parallel investigations into the still-unfolding event.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

The security team's efforts to identify the attacker by tracing registry ownership, npm maintainer history, publisher identities, and GitHub records quickly led them to dead ends. The repository had been copied from a legitimate project, and the publisher's identity and account history appeared to have been fabricated, Kanjani said.

Researchers have subsequently attributed at least some of the later Shai-Hulud attacks to a threat actor tracked as TeamPCP.

The key takeaway, according to Kanjani, is that organizations need to look beyond SBOMs and dependency inventories and instead base incident response around what actually runs in production. The focus should be to equip security teams to identify, scope, prioritize, and contain incidents and enable real-time visibility into affected services and the potential scope of a compromise.

"You are triaging a runtime graph. Not a dependency file. Your tools must reflect that," he said.

Kanjani recommended that organizations keep deployed SBOMs under 72 hours old and try to ensure that more than 98% of production services meet that threshold. He also recommended enabling runtime capabilities to detect unknown module loads in under 90 seconds and daily registry checks to detect lookalikes of internal package names within 24 hours of publication.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Kanjani described these as targets that organizations should calibrate for their own environments rather than as universal benchmarks. In addition, security teams should focus on the operation rather than the operator, Kanjani said. "Identity signals rotate. Operational necessities don't. Build detection around what the worm must do to function — not who's driving it."

All communications with stakeholders regarding a security incident also need to be direct and unambiguous. The key is to be honest, he said, while making sure to present the details in language appropriate for the intended audience.

"Don't bullsh-t. Tell them the reality in a way they can absorb it," he said. "You don't want to sell panic."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

If this is your idea, then I can understand your pov about (L)GPL and free software in general.

There are many projects with BSD/MIT licences that are successful and alive and some of them (like LLVM) have even significantly eroded their GPL competition.

Specifically, in LLVM's case, this is precisely because many companies have their internal forks and closed versions of LLVM and only give back the patches which doesn't affect their position regarding to their closed source versions, and can work with others' patches.

In other words, LLVM is one of the *ium projects (e.g. VSCode / VSCodium, Chrome/Chromium) as I call it. For example, IIRC, Intel moved their compiler suite under LLVM, but that version is not open source, either.

GCC suite is specifically designed at software level and licensed that way to prevent this.

Put in other terms, many projects are licensed with MIT to allow their developers to be hired by a company to create a career over that piece of code, and spread in software ecosystem to create a dependency to the developer responsible for the code.

Lastly, because of these dynamics, MIT is about developer freedom and GPL is about user freedom. I personally care about user freedom way more than developer freedom.

The license requires: > The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all copies or substantial portions of the Software. The GPLv2 is quite a bit wordier, but it's basically the same idea: > [...] provided that you conspicuously and appropriately publish on each copy an appropriate copyright notice and disclaimer of warranty; keep intact all the notices that refer to this License and to the absence of any warranty [...] Neither license prevents rebranding (in my opinion it's a real weakness of free software licenses). Both require minimal attribution in the form of a copyright notice, but not more. Neither prevents aggressive monetization. I guess the GPL makes it easier to prove that some downstream is in fact based on the project, if they comply with the license and publish source code. But what are you going to do once you prove that? Issue a takedown? For what license violation? When it comes to LLM rewrites, perhaps the GPL is a bit clearer about applying to "a work based on the Program" even if it does not contain (as MIT puts it) "substantial portions of the Software". But I'm skeptical that there's a real legal difference. The main difference the GPL makes, of course, is that the Asahi project could theoretically incorporate changes from downstream back into the project. That is the GPL's reason for existing. But in this case, the Asahi project describes the downstream code as "lazily rewritten", as using "LLM assistance" (which the Asahi project bans), and as being prematurely-released copies of their "in-development" code. It really doesn't sound like they have any interest in using it. So I'm somewhat mystified what the GPL is supposed to accomplish. That said, I have no firsthand knowledge of the downstreams they're talking about.

Modern Free Software licences now try to extend their grasp beyond copyright, and imho that is a BIG mistake. Neither patents, nor branding, are anything to do with copyright. And blocking re-branding would pretty much kill Free Software! If you can't rebrand then either (a) the only person able to distribute is the guy who originally wrote the project, or (b) anybody can modify the project but they have to keep the original name, and therefore they sink the project's reputation. Branding is your guarantee of "the genuine article". You NEED branding. You NEED trademarks. And you NEED to allow people to protect their reputation. Forcing people to remove your branding/trademarks from their derivative works is just normal honest business - it's NOT removing them that's dishonest. Cheers, Wol

I've seen some people go with MIT or BSD and then get annoyed at somebody building a proprietary project on top or not giving back, and this always confused me. If you see that as a problem, then use something stronger. It's weird for me to choose something permissive then expect people (and especially amoral organizations) to abide by some code of niceness. IMO if you expect people to reciprocate it's best to make it upfront and explicit.

IMO if you expect people to reciprocate it's best to make it upfront and explicit.

Does MIT allow forking without attribution? No, not it does not. You have to say that you are using code based on the MIT license. The requirement to attribute copyright reveals the original authors and the existance of the original project code. Does it allow you to "monetize without giving back"? Well, let's talk about that. The MIT license allows you to sell compiled binaries. So, "yes" to monetizing. The GPL also allows this. No difference. BOTH licenses require you to disclose whose code you are using because you have to attribute copyright to them. So your ability to monetize can be held in check by the "consumers" ability to compare what you are selling with the "free" alternative. In other words, you can only really "monetize" the value of what you provide above and beyond the MIT code you are using. If you are not adding any value, a "rational" consumer can choose the free alternative. The choice of GPL vs MIT does not really make much difference in terms of competing with forks that do not add any value. If you are just going to recompile the code and sell it, there is not that much difference between MIT and GPL really. If you are a fork, the GPL requires you to directly distribute the source code yourself. MIT does not require that. But MIT requires you to reveal that the MIT project (and code) exists so that people can go get it themselves from somebody else that is distributing it. In my view, there is not much difference when we are talking about just blanket copying a project and redistributing it or even trying to sell it. So, I must say, the concerns made by Asahi about low quality, low effort competition or peope trying to take their work to obscure origin or to restribute without attribution do not seem to be addressed at all by the change in license from MIT to GPL? So, what about "giving back"? This is where MIT and GPL do differ. The risk of permissive licenses is that the original project may lose popularity in head-to-head competition with rivals that are making changes and adding value that would make people choose the fork over the original. Whether this is ok or not is up to the original author of the code. Choosing MIT says that you are ok with this. If you are not, don't choose MIT. But be honest that your concern is more about popularity than it is about "freedom". Because it is only the stuff that your competitors are offering and you are not that puts you at a disadvantage. The GPL makes it harder for forks to compete. It does this by making it harder for them to add value on top of the project that will make them more attractive than the original project. It does not make it any harder for them to use the original code. See above. However, the "fork" has to make its "improvements" available to the orignal project as well. If those changes are valuable, the original project can incorporate them too. So, let's be clear. The choice of license between MIT and GPL is not really about the code you are placing under an Open Source license. That code is equally free and available to all in either case. The MIT code is perhaps even more "free" if we view the "permissive" nature as freedom. Both licenses require the code that already exists to be available and both licenses require that the users of the software know that the code is avaialble. The difference between the licenses comes into play when a fork adds changes on top of the original project. In GPL projects, those changes also have to be made available in source code form to both the users of the software and to the original source code project. With a permissive license like MIT, those changes do NOT have to be shared. The example given about WINE is instructive. The issue then was that CodeWeavers, a commercial WINE backer, did not like that Cedega (a competitor to CodeWeavers) was selling "improved" versions of WINE but not making their changes available to WINE and to CodeWeavers. It was not about the MIT code. It was about the "not MIT" code. As Asahi is non-commercial, it is less clear to me what damages they are trying to protect against here. Selling low-quality derivatives without attribution is no harder under either license. If that is what poeple are doing, they may well continue to do so, GPL or no GPL. What this change may protect against is to insulate Asahi from competition that actually IS adding value that they are not. But that is not the way they are framing it. A key consideration is that the users and the engineers may disagree on what "value" is. In particular, consider AI assissted changes on top of the original Asahi project. Users may like these changes and prefer the fork. There may be "value" in the eyes of users. But the Asahi devs may see these changes as "low value" if they think the code is low value or low effort (or low ethics depending on your view on AI). But how does a switch to GPL impact this case? If users are going to be attracted to forks that based on "AI slop" in the view of the Ashai devs, does the GPL help them? Are they going to incorporate these changes into Asahi? If not, how does the GPL help them? It may not. Perhaps what they are hoping for is to trap lazy competitors. If I make a "low effort" Ashai clone with additional AI features addded, I may be too lazy or too disorganized to comply with the GPL. The fact that I do not share my changes may make it easier for Asahi as a GPL violation is a clear-cut thing to try to enforce. But what is the remedy? If a low-effort fork pushes code to GitHub, does that change anything? We will see. Anwway, Asahi is an awesome project. They are doing amazing work and a lot of WORK. They can of course choose the license that suits them. My statements are questions are not meant to be negative towards the Asahi project in any way.

If you are not adding any value, a "rational" consumer can choose the free alternative. The choice of GPL vs MIT does not really make much difference in terms of competing with forks that do not add any value. If you are just going to recompile the code and sell it, there is not that much difference between MIT and GPL really. If you are a fork, the GPL requires you to directly distribute the source code yourself. MIT does not require that. But MIT requires you to reveal that the MIT project (and code) exists so that people can go get it themselves from somebody else that is distributing it. In my view, there is not much difference when we are talking about just blanket copying a project and redistributing it or even trying to sell it. So, I must say, the concerns made by Asahi about low quality, low effort competition or peope trying to take their work to obscure origin or to restribute without attribution do not seem to be addressed at all by the change in license from MIT to GPL? So, what about "giving back"? This is where MIT and GPL do differ. The risk of permissive licenses is that the original project may lose popularity in head-to-head competition with rivals that are making changes and adding value that would make people choose the fork over the original. Whether this is ok or not is up to the original author of the code. Choosing MIT says that you are ok with this. If you are not, don't choose MIT. But be honest that your concern is more about popularity than it is about "freedom". Because it is only the stuff that your competitors are offering and you are not that puts you at a disadvantage. The GPL makes it harder for forks to compete. It does this by making it harder for them to add value on top of the project that will make them more attractive than the original project. It does not make it any harder for them to use the original code. See above. However, the "fork" has to make its "improvements" available to the orignal project as well. If those changes are valuable, the original project can incorporate them too. So, let's be clear. The choice of license between MIT and GPL is not really about the code you are placing under an Open Source license. That code is equally free and available to all in either case. The MIT code is perhaps even more "free" if we view the "permissive" nature as freedom. Both licenses require the code that already exists to be available and both licenses require that the users of the software know that the code is avaialble. The difference between the licenses comes into play when a fork adds changes on top of the original project. In GPL projects, those changes also have to be made available in source code form to both the users of the software and to the original source code project. With a permissive license like MIT, those changes do NOT have to be shared. The example given about WINE is instructive. The issue then was that CodeWeavers, a commercial WINE backer, did not like that Cedega (a competitor to CodeWeavers) was selling "improved" versions of WINE but not making their changes available to WINE and to CodeWeavers. It was not about the MIT code. It was about the "not MIT" code. As Asahi is non-commercial, it is less clear to me what damages they are trying to protect against here. Selling low-quality derivatives without attribution is no harder under either license. If that is what poeple are doing, they may well continue to do so, GPL or no GPL. What this change may protect against is to insulate Asahi from competition that actually IS adding value that they are not. But that is not the way they are framing it. A key consideration is that the users and the engineers may disagree on what "value" is. In particular, consider AI assissted changes on top of the original Asahi project. Users may like these changes and prefer the fork. There may be "value" in the eyes of users. But the Asahi devs may see these changes as "low value" if they think the code is low value or low effort (or low ethics depending on your view on AI). But how does a switch to GPL impact this case? If users are going to be attracted to forks that based on "AI slop" in the view of the Ashai devs, does the GPL help them? Are they going to incorporate these changes into Asahi? If not, how does the GPL help them? It may not. Perhaps what they are hoping for is to trap lazy competitors. If I make a "low effort" Ashai clone with additional AI features addded, I may be too lazy or too disorganized to comply with the GPL. The fact that I do not share my changes may make it easier for Asahi as a GPL violation is a clear-cut thing to try to enforce. But what is the remedy? If a low-effort fork pushes code to GitHub, does that change anything? We will see. Anwway, Asahi is an awesome project. They are doing amazing work and a lot of WORK. They can of course choose the license that suits them. My statements are questions are not meant to be negative towards the Asahi project in any way.

Whether this is ok or not is up to the original author of the code. Choosing MIT says that you are ok with this. If you are not, don't choose MIT. But be honest that your concern is more about popularity than it is about "freedom". Because it is only the stuff that your competitors are offering and you are not that puts you at a disadvantage. The GPL makes it harder for forks to compete. It does this by making it harder for them to add value on top of the project that will make them more attractive than the original project. It does not make it any harder for them to use the original code. See above. However, the "fork" has to make its "improvements" available to the orignal project as well. If those changes are valuable, the original project can incorporate them too. So, let's be clear. The choice of license between MIT and GPL is not really about the code you are placing under an Open Source license. That code is equally free and available to all in either case. The MIT code is perhaps even more "free" if we view the "permissive" nature as freedom. Both licenses require the code that already exists to be available and both licenses require that the users of the software know that the code is avaialble. The difference between the licenses comes into play when a fork adds changes on top of the original project. In GPL projects, those changes also have to be made available in source code form to both the users of the software and to the original source code project. With a permissive license like MIT, those changes do NOT have to be shared. The example given about WINE is instructive. The issue then was that CodeWeavers, a commercial WINE backer, did not like that Cedega (a competitor to CodeWeavers) was selling "improved" versions of WINE but not making their changes available to WINE and to CodeWeavers. It was not about the MIT code. It was about the "not MIT" code. As Asahi is non-commercial, it is less clear to me what damages they are trying to protect against here. Selling low-quality derivatives without attribution is no harder under either license. If that is what poeple are doing, they may well continue to do so, GPL or no GPL. What this change may protect against is to insulate Asahi from competition that actually IS adding value that they are not. But that is not the way they are framing it. A key consideration is that the users and the engineers may disagree on what "value" is. In particular, consider AI assissted changes on top of the original Asahi project. Users may like these changes and prefer the fork. There may be "value" in the eyes of users. But the Asahi devs may see these changes as "low value" if they think the code is low value or low effort (or low ethics depending on your view on AI). But how does a switch to GPL impact this case? If users are going to be attracted to forks that based on "AI slop" in the view of the Ashai devs, does the GPL help them? Are they going to incorporate these changes into Asahi? If not, how does the GPL help them? It may not. Perhaps what they are hoping for is to trap lazy competitors. If I make a "low effort" Ashai clone with additional AI features addded, I may be too lazy or too disorganized to comply with the GPL. The fact that I do not share my changes may make it easier for Asahi as a GPL violation is a clear-cut thing to try to enforce. But what is the remedy? If a low-effort fork pushes code to GitHub, does that change anything? We will see. Anwway, Asahi is an awesome project. They are doing amazing work and a lot of WORK. They can of course choose the license that suits them. My statements are questions are not meant to be negative towards the Asahi project in any way.

No, MIT license do not require to disclose your code, it only mandates to preserve attribution and the legal notice. But if you change just the 10% of the code and leave the remaining 90% unchanged then you can keep all the source private as long as you give attribution of the remaining part.

I don't think the second part is true. Yes GPL requires providing source code to those who receive binaries but it does not, according to my understanding, require providing the code to the original project. Of course it also disallows forbidding recipients of the binary and source from providing the source to others. So if a commercial "imprroved" Ashai were made under the GPL Ashai would not automatically get the modifications. But anyonoe who purchased a copy of it would get the source code and would be allowed to share it with Ashai.

1. Work with a qualified lawyer (aka specializes in software licensing ) on what the problem is and what the solutions could be 2. Follow the lawyer’s advice on how to relicense things. 3. Work with the lawyer on how to announce and describe the issue. There can be specific reasons why a specific license is seen as 'stronger' in different countries or court systems to get the effects you are wanting. [Attribution can mean different things in different countries and some court systems may like X license over Y license for some obscure reason that the lawyers can make clear.] This is probably something that should be on the list early in any project. Even if you are going to select MIT-0 or BSD-0 , getting an idea of why you are doing this and what you can expect as benefits or trouble is good.

#9856. External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Mail bombing is getting a new look with a wide-scale, ongoing social engineering campaign that might be tied to the Black Basta ransomware gang.

Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams' external chat functionality at scale, using IT-support impersonation and email bombing tactics to trick employees into granting remote access. Attackers target multiple users within short, five-minute windows of time, and once the victim bites, the attack chain reaches payload execution in under 15 minutes.

In a blog post on Oct. 26, Arctic Wolf detailed the campaign and what it described as a "recurring social engineering pattern" across more than 400 incidents in the wild. Threat actors use Microsoft Teams' external chat creation capability, which enables outside parties to contact employees.

"A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same 'IT Support (Internal)' display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains," Arctic Wolf's Shubham Dubey wrote in the blog post.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

In a typical example of the attack, the victim is "mail bombed," or inundated with a flood of email subscriptions or newsletters, to establish a sense of urgency. Then, an external Teams user claiming to be IT support contacts the victim and offers to address the issue. The impersonator persuades the employee to launch a remote-access session via legitimate tooling like Quick Assist (most common), AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn.

Once the victim grants access, the attacker conducts follow-on activity such as executing malware, stealing credentials, performing reconnaissance, or possibly deploying ransomware. Dubey explained that a typical order for this is a whoami/systeminfo-based recon, a PowerShell-based payload, a command-and-control (2) beacon, lateral movement to gain access to credentials through Kerberos abuse methods like Kerberoasting and GoldenPAC, and a second, commercial-grade remote access tool, "which provides an independent control channel that survives remediation of the original implant."

Spam or mail bombing is not a new tactic. Threat actors have been flooding inboxes as a pretense for social engineering for some time now. Microsoft researchers identified the use of this technique by Black Basta in mid-2024, with later examples seen in 3AM, Cactus, Chaos, and the GoGRPC campaigns. But what stands out about Arctic Wolf's research is that it shows this technique operating at scale, with recurring infrastructure, naming conventions, and attacker behavior seen across hundreds of incidents.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading roughly 15% of cases progressed beyond the initial stage into a successful compromise, which, given the volume of the campaign, constitutes a success.

As for who is behind recent attack waves, Moore could not make definitive attributions but says, "Black Basta-associated activity remains one of the most significant drivers of Teams chat abuse."

On the infrastructure front, Arctic Wolf noted a move from throwaway onmicrosoft.com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, especially ".top" domains, and provided data on their prevalence. The vendor stated that approximately half of observed cases involving paid domains used .top domains.

For naming, attackers would reach out with "(Internal)" appended to the display name to trick the victim that a message is coming from within the company, even though Teams labels the sender as "external" simultaneously. The names will also frequently use friendly sounding names (Arctic Wolf offered Liam, Scott McGhee, and Matthew as examples) after labels like "IT Support" and "IT Service Desk."

Other markers observed included naming conventions specific to the target's locale ("Supporte TI" for French- and Spanish-speaking organizations), and the use of 100 different emojis in attacker display names.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

Arctic Wolf noted that prior to engaging with victims, the attackers initiate a one-on-one chat to avoid group conversations, which Microsoft records in its telemetry as the ChatCreated event. Arctic Wolf assesses this to be the primary detection point for defenders setting alerts.

The vendor also recommended setting an allowlist for trusted external organizations, blocking chats with unmanaged or Teams consumer accounts, disabling the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users, blocking federation with trial-only tenants, and hardening your remote access path.

In a nod to Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Arctic Wolf pointed out that it may also be wise to alert staff to the social engineering aspects behind these campaigns, including outlining exactly how IT reaches out, what these contacts look like (and what they do not look like), and to train users how to read the external sender tag in Teams to identify possible red flags. Microsoft Teams also includes end-user reporting in the application itself.

That said, the technique could yet progress further.

"We have also recently observed campaigns combining Teams chat abuse with ClickFix-style social engineering, suggesting that the technique continues to evolve and is being integrated with other intrusion methods," Moore says.

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading that the company helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through layered, built-in protections that, for example, can let administrators block external Teams users. The spokesperson adds that, next month, "Teams is introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users."

He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

#9855. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.
