Edoardo Vacchi: No, no, it is correct on a high level. More specifically, so VLLM is our inference engine. So, you can think of it, if you will, as the JVM of language models. So, it has support for several language models, there's an interesting aside here, it is a platform to run LLMs. The interesting aside here is you would expect that this is a general sort of VM, and the LLMs are sort of software that you load on top of it. But unfortunately every LLM architecture is slightly different. So, VLLM has to basically include the implementation of every LLM that gets released. So, when people release LLMs, they do not release the software to run them, they release the weights. So, all of these inference engines, such as VLLM, what they do is implementing basically the software, the kernels, the components that actually load the weights and then actually do the inference.

So, VLLM is our platform to run the core and effectively VLLM is able to serve, it's a server... I mean, it's an inference engine, it's also server that exposes endpoints that you can call to do inference, and it does so efficiently. It was originally VLLM, I think the V in VLLM originally stands for virtual, as in virtual memory allocation. Because it was the first engine to implement page detention, basically a mechanism inspired by good old systems programming to do paging of memory, memory pages, but for memory that gets allocated on GPU, this is in a very high level way. So, VLLM is able to do high throughput inference. So, you can do several requests at once and VLLM will pack them and try to serve them together, and do inference in one pass for several requests at one time, this is called continuous batching. But this gets you to a point.

Essentially, at some point you have your GPUs on your machine, and your inference engine and that's it. You will not be able to scale further than the resources that you have on that machine. So, how do you scale further? Well, you can scale by having more VLLM instances, right? So, you have several VLLM instances and you want to serve your inference requests using these few VLLM, these few VLLM instances that you have. Now, you have another problem. How do you route requests across your VLLM instances? So, if you are on Kubernetes, what you will do... And most people are on Kubernetes these days, it's the standard for platforms for serving services in an efficient way. So, you can scale your VLLM instances and have several VLLM instances that serve the possible the same request... I mean that gets selected by the scheduler, by the VLLM scheduler.

If you do it the traditional way and let the Kubernetes normal router to pick across the VLLM instances that you have replicated, you won't get necessarily good performance. The reason is inference does not behave like a traditional service, a traditional HTP service. Basically, if you send a request to one specific VLLM instance, especially if you are doing conversation, if you're doing a chat and if you're doing agentic coding, it's still a chat basically. There's a lot of exchanges back and forth between you and your server, between your agent and your server. You want to stick for as much time as possible to the same VLLM instance. This might be counterintuitive in a way because for microservices, we know we don't want to hammer the same service on and on because otherwise it will get overloaded. We want to do sort of round robbing or random robbing across the replicas.

But the thing is microservices or service in general, these are usually in a way stateless. The state is usually stored somewhere else and it's not part of your request. I mean, the request can be served independently by any instance. Unfortunately for LLMs, in order for LLMs to do their inference in an efficient way, you want to stick for as much time as possible to the same instance. But at the same time, you cannot stick forever to the same instance because at some point you will reach some limit. You are not the only user of that VLLM instance. You want to serve and distribute the load across your VLLM instances. So there's a balance that you have to strike between staying with the same instance and benefit of the caches, the KV caches, the prefix caches that are in place, the systems that allow you to do inference in an efficient way and lower costs.

But at the same time, you don't want to overload the same instance too much. So you also have to keep this into account. This is not the job for a traditional Kubernetes schedule. And that's where llm-d comes into place. That's what llm-d does. llm-d is not just a router or a scheduler. It's actually a family of projects and they are all meant to give you a set of tools to do distributed inference so that you can leverage all of the GPUs that you have and use it at their maximum as much as possible so you get the best value, the best bang for your bucks because these hardware is expensive whether you loan it or you own it. So you want to use it 100% as much as possible. And that's why we provide scheduler. We have something that we're going to release. I mean, in the open source ecosystem, it's already been released.

We're going to release also as part of product of Red Hat. This is called batch inference. Batch inference is using your cluster even when it's under load. So you can schedule request to do batch processing in the background when your cluster is underused because basically this hardware is so expensive that you want to keep it at 100% all the time. So even when there is no live inference going on, you can schedule batch processing to run when you're sleeping when there's less work to be done live. So that's what llm-d does. It uses your hardware as much as possible so that the money you spend gets you the best value and you do it on your own hardware so you can do inference without leaking data to a third party, which is important these days.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. It allows you to make cloud native inference and evolve your infrastructure in such a way that you can do AI on-premises, in a similar way as you did cloud native development before AI.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, to the conclusion earlier. And I said a lot about prefix caches and KV caches, but yes. So, essentially the way an LLM works is that essentially you always send the entirety of the conversation to the LLM. And what really happens is the LLM completes the conversation. I don't know if people recall how OpenAI and the GPT Lab playground worked a few years ago. Basically, it was the completion API. You wrote a sentence and then the LLM wrote the continuation of that. And the cool thing was that someone discovered if you wrote that prompt as a conversation, as a dialogue with quotes, user says da, da, da, computer says... The LLM will continue the conversation. And that's how ChatGPT basically was born. People notice this, and notice this pattern.

Now, LLMs are being trained with this pattern, but that's how basically originally it work. So, if you think of it this way, every conversation really is a very long prompt to the continuation of that conversation. The way LLM works, you send the history of the conversation and then they continue with the next answer, and then you get back the answer, and then you continue with your answer, and so on, so forth, so on and so forth. If you are using LLMs, you will know that pricing for these things, depending if you're using token-based spend or a subscription... Well, if you're using a subscription, that doesn't really matter. But if you're using token-based pricing, you will know that there's a difference between cached responses and responses.

The reason is, if you don't do a cached response, then you are sending the entire history of your conversation to the LLM. The LLM does not have that conversation in cache, so it will have to do inference on the entire prompt, and that's why that will be particularly expensive. But if you've been going back and forth for a while without long pauses and the cache on the server has not been evicted, then you've been reusing stored cache estate to continue the conversation. That does not mean necessarily that you haven't sent the entire history to the LLM, it just means that even though you are sending the entire history, the history is recognized as part of a prefix of a cache, and so the LLM can compute only the continuation instead of the entire prompt.

So, we have these mechanism for caching in place so that basically LLMs, if the cache exists, can only infer the last few tokens that continue the conversation instead of have to re-compute the entire state from the prompt. llm-d does that for you. So, it maintains this cache both in the form of a KV cache, with one going to the deals how that works, and a prefix cache. And both these caching mechanism allow you to persist the state across the exchanges in your conversation, persist as in volatile memory because these are caches... Usually they're not persistent for a long time. And that's the reason also why you want to stick usually to the same VLLM instance, even though llm-d also gives you ways to move around across instances. It's a lot, we cannot explain how all that works. But in general, llm-d allows you to do this, allows you to have an efficient use and even for stateful conversation of your hardware.

Organizations may not be ready for completely autonomous communication processes, but there are places where automating information updates would alleviate pressure.

Organizations steadily deploy automated threat detection and response processes; some even take it a step further with fully artificial intelligence (AI) security operations centers (SOCs). Automation can catch an incident in seconds, yet communication remains mostly manual across an industry that requires more transparency.

The disconnect can strain relationships and trust as customers wait for incident impact and mitigation answers. Hands-on communications also put more pressure on chief information security officers (CISOs), who must relay timely updates to IT personnel and executives as the incident clock winds down.

Incident response (IR) communications are increasingly too much for humans to coordinate without more help. But disclosures contain sensitive information — the status of a company's security posture or how they responded when alerted to an incident — and automation takes away some of the control leadership wants to hold onto in regard to timing and specifics.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

From a coordination and information standpoint, automating communications is absolutely important, says Tim Brown, chief strategy officer at Cytactic. That could mean implementing a centralized place to view everyone's status versus relying on meetings to receive updates.

A dedicated crisis communication platform could help, Brown says. A single click of a button could notify everyone, and that includes contingency options if normal communications go down, which is typical following an incident where systems go offline.

Brown is no stranger to hectic IR communication scenarios. While trying to manage the SolarWinds attack fallout, the former CISO got pulled into one crisis after the other. He oversaw five different teams, coordinated tasks, scheduled meetings, received updates from everyone, and tried to keep the customers briefed.

As he looks back now, he appreciates how much help everyone around him was. Still, some preparation was missing: more tabletop exercises, meeting the appropriate people beforehand, and technology to ease communications.

IR communications are complicated. Organizations may wait to disclose certain information, so they do not tip off attackers. Sometimes victim organizations post customer-only private advisories, but that leaves public awareness and downstream victims vulnerable. Yet other times, companies simply choose not to disclose or downplay effects to save face.

The Securities and Exchange Commission and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) continue to update and adopt new disclosure regulations in light of more disruptive attacks. The Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) of 2022, after missing several earlier deadlines, is nearing finalization. Once in effect, the rule would require covered entities to report substantial cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours of discovery, and critical infrastructure organizations that make ransom payments would need to report within 24 hours.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Even if organizations want to disclose any information in good faith, that poses challenges. A wide net of victims, third parties, and supply chain risks abound. It's increasingly more difficult to even know who is affected these days.

Douglas McKee, director of vulnerability intelligence at Rapid7, ventures to guess that most security leaders would cite communication problems, and they usually exist long before an incident ever happens. For example, security teams tend to talk in terms of common vulnerability exposures (CVEs) and indicators of compromise, while the people making business decisions need to know what any of that actually means.

On a normal day, that gap is annoying, but during an incident, the language barrier gets amplified because everyone needs answers at the same moment, even though the facts change by the hour. And nobody wants to be the person who said the wrong thing publicly, McKee adds.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

"Third parties make this even harder," he tells Dark Reading. "I've seen plenty of situations where a vendor knows about a problem in their product well before their customers do, but the notification lands in a generic inbox or goes to a contact who left the company two years ago.”

Attackers benefit from that confusion, he notes, adding how important it is for defenders to agree internally on what's happening so they can relay information to customers confidently.

Organizations want to be more transparent but continually struggle with how to personalize communication outreach, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Whether in day-to-day fraud communications or during an active incident, the more they can leverage AI, insights, and understanding the better they can adapt, he adds .

Right now, it's easier to automate detection and response because the inputs can be fairly structured, explains McKee; a log entry either matches a rule or it doesn't. IR communication, on the other hand, involves judgement calls with legal and reputational consequences.

"Organizations are understandably nervous about letting a machine decide what goes out the door with their name on it," McKee says. "Let's face it: An analyst can shrug off a false positive in a few minutes, but there's no easy way to 'unsend' an inaccurate breach notice to your customers."

That doesn't mean automating communication is off the table — it just needs to be pointed at the right parts of the problem, he says. Organizations can automate pulling together the incident timeline or tracking which stakeholders have been notified and when. McKee also recommends using tools to draft a first version of an update from data the responders already have.

It's all about freeing people up to spend their time on decisions that actually need a human. The way McKee looks at it, "automation should get the draft in front of the right person faster, and that person should still be the one who verifies and hits send."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9770. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#9769. How to Trace AI Agent Decisions Across Blockchain Transactions

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

A blockchain transaction can tell us what happened. It cannot, by itself, explain why an AI agent decided to initiate it. Imagine an AI agent monitoring a decentralised finance application. It reads wallet balances, retrieves liquidity data, evaluates a possible transaction, calls a smart contract, and waits for confirmation. Eventually, the transaction appears on-chain. A monitoring dashboard shows its hash, gas consumption, status, and block number. Everything looks normal.

Then someone notices that the transaction moved assets into a position the user never intended to create. Where did things go wrong? Perhaps the agent interpreted an instruction incorrectly. Perhaps an RPC provider returned stale information. Perhaps the market changed after the agent calculated the expected outcome. Perhaps a policy check passed against an outdated configuration. Or perhaps the transaction executed exactly as designed, but the design itself failed to account for an important condition.

The transaction hash does not answer these questions. Neither does a conventional application log that says a tool call succeeded. To investigate the incident, engineers need to reconstruct the complete path from the original instruction to the final on-chain state. They need to understand which information the agent observed, how it interpreted that information, what action it proposed, which controls approved the action, and what happened during execution. This is where I believe observability needs to evolve.

My work and writing around production AI have repeatedly brought me back to a distinction that is easy to overlook: making a system capable of performing a task is not the same as making its behaviour understandable when something goes wrong. AI agents introduce additional uncertainty because they can select tools, generate plans, and change their approach based on intermediate results. Blockchain introduces another layer of complexity through asynchronous transactions, external data dependencies, network conditions, and state changes that may be difficult or impossible to reverse. Combining the two creates a system that needs visibility into both reasoning-related decisions and deterministic execution.

Blockchain applications need an observability layer that connects what an AI agent intended to do with what the infrastructure actually executed. That layer should not attempt to expose every internal model computation or turn private reasoning into an audit log. It should capture the operational evidence needed to explain decisions, enforce policies, investigate failures, and verify outcomes.

Traditional blockchain monitoring has a well-understood job. It tracks transactions, blocks, contract events, network health, gas usage, and other indicators of execution. These measurements remain essential. They tell us whether transactions were submitted, whether they were included in a block, whether execution succeeded, and how the network behaved. But consider what happens before an AI-generated transaction reaches the blockchain.

An agent receives a request, retrieves context, calls one or more tools, interprets their responses, evaluates possible actions, and produces a transaction proposal. That proposal passes through authorisation, signing, and submission before the blockchain processes it. Every stage can introduce a different failure. The agent may select the wrong contract. A retrieval service may provide outdated protocol information. An RPC provider may become unavailable. A policy engine may reject a valid transaction because it received malformed input. A signer may refuse an operation that exceeded their authorisation. The transaction may be accepted by an RPC endpoint but remain pending, or it may be included in a block and revert during execution.

A dashboard focused exclusively on the blockchain sees only part of this journey. Likewise, an AI application log may record that the model proposed a swap without establishing whether the proposal was authorised, signed, submitted, or confirmed. The problem is not that either monitoring system is inadequate within its own domain. The problem is that the two systems often describe different parts of the same operation without a shared way to connect them. An AI-native observability layer bridges that gap. It connects the original request, the agent's operational decisions, the data used to support those decisions, the policy checks, the transaction lifecycle, and the resulting on-chain state. The goal is not to replace blockchain explorers, node metrics, or application monitoring. It is to connect their evidence into a single operational picture.

Logs are useful for recording individual events. A service might log that it retrieved a balance, generated a transaction proposal, or received a transaction receipt. The difficulty begins when an operation crosses several services.

Suppose an agent retrieves data through an RPC gateway, obtains additional information from an indexer, sends a proposal to a policy service, and submits an approved transaction through a signing service. Each component produces its own logs, often with its own request identifiers and timestamps.

During an incident, engineers may have to search several systems and manually reconstruct the order of events. If an intermediate request was retried, if a response arrived late, or if the agent resumed a workflow after a timeout, that reconstruction becomes even harder. A timestamp alone is not enough to establish causality. Two events can occur close together without belonging to the same workflow, while events from one workflow may appear out of order because different services process them asynchronously.

This is why distributed tracing is a useful foundation. OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral model for collecting traces, metrics, and logs across instrumented services. A trace can represent a larger operation, while individual spans describe the work performed by its components. For a blockchain-connected agent, one trace might represent the attempt to execute a particular user request. Its spans could include context retrieval, transaction planning, policy evaluation, simulation, signing authorisation, RPC submission, and receipt verification. The resulting trace gives engineers a structured way to understand how the operation progressed. However, a trace alone does not establish that the operation was correct. It establishes the relationships between recorded operations and helps reveal where failures or delays occurred.

The observability layer must therefore combine tracing with domain-specific information: transaction identifiers, chain and block references, policy versions, execution status, and the outcome that the user originally requested.

I would design the architecture around six connected layers.

The diagram represents a logical architecture rather than a requirement to deploy every component as a separate service. A small application might implement several layers within one process. A larger platform may distribute them across multiple services. What matters is that each stage has a defined responsibility and emits enough structured evidence for the next stage to be observed.

The runtime records when an agent begins a task, which tools it invokes, how long each operation takes, and whether the agent produces a proposal or requests additional information. For example, the runtime might record that an agent evaluated three transaction routes, rejected two under its configured constraints, and selected the third for further validation.

It does not need to capture the private chain of thought or every intermediate token. It needs a concise operational record of the decisions and outputs that matter to the workflow.

The context layer records where decision-relevant information came from. For blockchain data, useful attributes may include the chain ID, block number, block hash, source provider, observation timestamp, and indexing checkpoint, where applicable.

These attributes help engineers determine whether an agent acted on current and consistent information. A block number should not be treated as a universal freshness guarantee. The system must also consider the network's finality characteristics, the source's progress, and the requirements of the specific operation.

The policy layer records which rules were evaluated and whether the proposal passed. Useful fields include a policy version, the result of each relevant check, a machine-readable rejection reason, and whether additional authorisation was required. This allows an investigator to distinguish between an agent that proposed an invalid action and a policy engine that incorrectly authorised it.

Sensitive policy details should be access-controlled. The observability system should not become a convenient source of information for someone attempting to bypass security controls.

The execution layer records the transition from proposed transaction to authorisation, submission, inclusion, and verification. The distinction between these states matters. A successful RPC response does not necessarily mean that a transaction was confirmed. A receipt with a successful execution status is stronger evidence of execution, but the application may still need to verify that the resulting state satisfies the original goal.

The final layer compares the intended outcome with the observed result. If the agent intended to transfer a specified amount to an approved destination, the system should verify the relevant transaction and state changes rather than relying solely on a success message returned by the execution service. For more complex operations, such as adjusting a DeFi position, the expected outcome may involve several balances, contract events, and protocol-specific state variables.

The verification rules should be defined for the application rather than inferred solely from the model's natural-language summary.

Traces, metrics, and structured audit records feed dashboards, alerts, incident investigations, and recovery workflows. An alert might identify repeated RPC failures, a growing number of transactions stuck in a pending state, an increase in policy rejections, or a mismatch between confirmed transactions and expected business outcomes.

The objective is to move beyond reporting that something failed and toward identifying which boundary failed, what evidence supports that conclusion, and what safe action should happen next.

Consider a hypothetical agent that is asked to exchange a limited amount of a stablecoin for another asset. The agent retrieves the wallet balance, queries a liquidity pool, calculates an expected output, and proposes a swap. The policy engine checks the spending limit and slippage tolerance. A secure signer authorises the validated transaction, and an RPC endpoint submits it. A useful trace should preserve the relationships between these operations.

This trace is illustrative. In a real implementation, some stages may run concurrently, be retried, or occur in separate traces linked through workflow identifiers. The important feature is the relationship between them. An investigator should be able to start with a failed transaction and work backwards to the exact proposal, policy decision, and observations that supported it. Equally, the investigator should be able to start with an agent decision and follow it forward to the transaction's outcome.

A trace should also distinguish between attempts and logical operations. If an RPC request is retried three times, those attempts should remain visible without making them look like three separate user requests. This distinction becomes particularly valuable when agents resume long-running workflows. A workflow may survive a process restart, wait for a transaction to be included in a block, and continue later. Its operational history should remain connected even if its execution crosses several processes or sessions.

For a production system, I would use a durable workflow or operation identifier to connect the lifecycle, while creating spans for individual execution attempts. Where operations cross tracing boundaries, trace context can be propagated through service calls or linked explicitly. There is one important limitation: traces can be sampled, dropped, or retained for shorter periods than audit records. A security-sensitive application should not rely on sampled traces as its sole record of financial authorisation or execution.

Observability and auditability overlap, but they serve different purposes. Traces help engineers investigate behaviour. A durable audit record preserves the evidence required to establish what the system authorised and executed.

An observability design becomes more useful when it can be implemented with ordinary engineering tools. The following Python example uses OpenTelemetry-style instrumentation to create a trace for an agent's blockchain read. It illustrates how an application can associate a chain identifier and block reference with a request. The RPC response parsing and provider implementation are intentionally left outside the example because those depend on the application's client library.

This is a simplified instrumentation example, not a complete production RPC client. The actual method signature, block-reference format, and error handling must match the provider library being used.

It also deliberately avoids recording the wallet address or balance as unrestricted span attributes. Depending on the application, those values may be sensitive. A controlled internal identifier or appropriately protected audit record can provide correlation without exposing unnecessary financial information in telemetry. There is another useful distinction in this example: the block number is part of the operation's context, not merely a descriptive label. If the agent later creates a transaction based on that observation, the workflow can reference the observation record and evaluate whether the information is still valid for execution. The span tells us which read occurred. The associated decision record tells us why that read mattered.

A trace describes how work moved through the system. A decision record describes the operational basis for a consequential action. I would give every transaction proposal a durable identifier and record the relevant context, policy version, and outcome. The record should contain enough information to reconstruct the decision without depending on the original model conversation remaining available. For example:

The identifiers and block numbers here are fictional. The example illustrates a useful design choice: the agent's decision can be stopped before signing if the application determines that the indexed data does not satisfy the freshness requirement for the intended operation.

The record does not claim that every two-block difference is unsafe. Whether that difference matters depends on the chain, the indexer's behaviour, the transaction, and the application's consistency requirements. A reporting agent might accept the indexed observation. An agent preparing a price-sensitive swap might require a newer observation or an independent validation step. The decision record should make the distinction explicit. It should also be updated as the operation progresses, or linked to append-only lifecycle events, so that the system can distinguish between a proposal, an authorisation, a submission, and a verified outcome.

For high-impact operations, I prefer a design in which the authorisation event is separately recorded and bound to the exact transaction parameters. This reduces the risk that a proposal will be changed after it passes validation. A record should never be treated as proof that an action occurred merely because it says the action was intended. The execution evidence must be independently established.

One of the most common mistakes in monitoring is treating every unsuccessful operation as the same kind of failure. A failed RPC request, an agent decision rejected by policy, a transaction that reverts, and a successful transaction that produces the wrong business outcome are fundamentally different events. They require different responses. I would classify failures by the layer where they occur and the evidence needed to resolve them.

Refresh, reconcile, or reject the decision

The proposal does not satisfy the task constraints

Reject the proposal and investigate the planning failure

Block execution and record the violated rule

Apply bounded retry or use an approved alternative source

The transaction remains pending or is replaced

Reconcile the known transaction state before taking action

Inspect the receipt and relevant execution details

Transaction succeeds, but the intended result is not achieved

Trigger investigation and an application-specific recovery process

Required telemetry or audit evidence is missing

Raise a monitoring-integrity alert and apply the appropriate fail-safe policy

The category alone does not determine the response. A timeout might be transient, while a timeout during transaction submission may leave the outcome uncertain. A policy rejection may be the correct behaviour rather than an incident. The system should preserve the distinction between an expected refusal, a recoverable operational failure, and a security-relevant anomaly. This is particularly important for AI agents. If a system is evaluated only on its task-completion rate, it may appear that policy rejections are failures to be eliminated. In reality, a correctly rejected unsafe transaction can be a sign that the controls are working.

The right metric is not simply how often the agent completes a task. It is whether the system completes legitimate tasks while reliably preventing unauthorised or invalid actions.

An AI-native blockchain dashboard should help an operator answer three questions quickly:

I would organise the dashboard around those questions rather than presenting every available metric on one screen. The first view should show operational health: RPC latency, provider errors, indexer lag, agent task latency, queue depth, and transaction lifecycle distribution. The second should focus on decision integrity: stale-context rejections, inconsistent-observation detections, policy rejection reasons, simulation failures, and the proportion of transaction proposals requiring refresh or human approval. The third should focus on outcomes: pending transactions, confirmed execution results, reverted transactions, unresolved submissions, and mismatches between intended and observed state changes.

The following chart illustrates how a dashboard might compare decision outcomes over a hypothetical monitoring period. These are invented figures for demonstration, not measurements from a deployed system.

The value of this chart is not the particular proportions. Real systems will vary significantly by workload, protocol, and risk policy. The useful idea is that a single task success percentage conceals several different operational states.

For example, an increase in refresh-required proposals may indicate that an indexer is falling behind, that the application's freshness threshold is too strict, or that the workload has become more sensitive to rapidly changing data. A rise in unresolved submissions may indicate RPC instability or a problem with transaction-state reconciliation.

The dashboard should make it possible to move from a metric to the relevant traces and decision records. A number without a path to investigation is often a poor operational tool.

Observability is most useful when it helps teams identify a deteriorating condition before it becomes a serious incident. For blockchain-connected AI agents, I would start with a small set of operational indicators and expand them as the system's risks become better understood.

Context freshness. Measure the age of decision-critical observations at the time a proposal is authorised, not only when the data is retrieved. Where appropriate, measure the difference between the observation's block reference and the relevant indexing checkpoint.

Decision rejection rate. Track proposals rejected because of invalid assumptions, missing information, or policy violations. Break the metric down by reason so that an increase can be investigated rather than treated as a generic failure.

Transaction lifecycle latency. Measure time spent preparing, validating, signing, submitting, waiting for inclusion, and verifying outcomes. This helps distinguish slow agent reasoning from slow blockchain infrastructure.

Unresolved transaction rate. Track operations whose final state cannot yet be established. A pending or uncertain transaction should remain unresolved until the application has sufficient evidence to classify it.

Outcome mismatch rate. Measure how often an operation reaches a technically successful execution state without achieving its defined application-level objective.

Audit completeness. Measure whether consequential actions have the required decision, authorisation, transaction, and outcome records. Missing evidence is itself an operational concern.

These metrics should have explicit definitions. For example, an outcome mismatch rate needs a clear definition of success for each operation type. A token transfer may be verified through the relevant transaction and state changes, while a more complex DeFi operation may require several application-specific checks. Thresholds should also be established from the application's risk model and observed baseline rather than copied from an unrelated system.

I would avoid optimising the entire platform around one composite reliability score. Averages can hide rare but serious failures. A low average latency does not compensate for an unsafe transaction, and a high task-completion rate does not establish that authorisation controls are effective. For critical controls, direct measurements of violations and execution outcomes are more useful than a single headline number.

An observability platform can contain valuable information about how an AI agent operates, which contracts it interacts with, what policies constrain it, and how its execution infrastructure is configured. That information needs protection.

Logging every prompt, tool response, wallet identifier, and transaction parameter without considering their sensitivity can expose financial activity or reveal details that attackers could use to target the system. I would apply data minimisation at the instrumentation layer. Record the information required to understand a decision, but avoid collecting private keys, signing credentials, recovery phrases, or other secrets. Sensitive prompt content and user information should be redacted or access-controlled according to the application's requirements.

High-cardinality fields also deserve attention. Putting arbitrary wallet addresses, transaction hashes, or user identifiers into metric labels can cause monitoring systems to consume excessive memory and storage. These values are generally better suited to trace attributes or structured records than to unrestricted metric dimensions.

Audit integrity is another consideration. A system should make it difficult for an ordinary agent process to alter or delete the records of its own consequential actions. Depending on the threat model, this can involve append-only storage, restricted write permissions, integrity checks, and separation between the execution service and the audit service.

A hash-linked audit log can help detect certain forms of modification, but it does not automatically prove that the recorded events are complete or truthful. If the application fails to record an event in the first place, an integrity mechanism cannot reconstruct it.

Finally, observability must not silently become a dependency that fails open. If the system cannot produce a required authorisation record for a high-impact transaction, it may need to block execution or require a controlled fallback. For a low-risk reporting task, temporary telemetry loss might instead trigger an alert while the task continues. The correct response depends on the risk and on which records are essential to safe operation.

A full observability platform can become complicated quickly. It is tempting to instrument every service, define dozens of metrics, and build a large dashboard before understanding which questions the team actually needs to answer. I would start with one consequential workflow and instrument it end-to-end.

For example, select a transaction-preparation workflow that reads contract state, generates a proposal, applies policy checks, and submits an authorised transaction. Assign a stable workflow identifier, connect the relevant spans, and record the minimum decision and execution evidence.

Next, introduce controlled failure tests. Simulate an unavailable RPC provider, an indexer that falls behind, a policy rejection, a reverted transaction, and a submission timeout. Confirm that each scenario produces a distinct classification and that engineers can reconstruct the workflow without manually searching unrelated logs.

Then introduce the dashboard and define the expected behaviour for unresolved states. Ensure that an uncertain submission cannot trigger a duplicate transaction simply because an agent assumes the previous attempt failed. Only after these basics work would I expand the architecture to additional workflows and services. This approach makes observability an engineering capability that grows with the system rather than a separate reporting project. It also gives the team something measurable to improve: fewer unexplained failures, faster incident investigation, more complete decision records, and stronger evidence that authorisation and execution behave as intended.

As AI agents become more capable of interacting with financial infrastructure, the meaning of a successful operation will need to become more precise. A successful model response does not necessarily mean that a valid transaction was proposed. A successful RPC call does not mean that a transaction was confirmed. A confirmed transaction does not necessarily mean that the user's intended outcome was achieved.

Each stage needs its own evidence, and those stages need to remain connected. This is the architectural shift I find most important: moving from monitoring individual components to observing the complete lifecycle of an autonomous decision.

Blockchain explorers will continue to provide valuable visibility into on-chain activity. Application logs will continue to explain local execution. Distributed traces will continue to connect work across services. But AI-driven applications need an additional layer that connects those sources to the intent, constraints, and outcome of each consequential action.

That layer must also recognise its own limits. Observability can help engineers understand what happened, detect unexpected behaviour, and improve recovery. It cannot guarantee that an agent will never make a bad decision, replace a sound authorisation model, or reverse a transaction that has already been confirmed.

Its purpose is to make the system's behaviour sufficiently visible that problems can be detected, investigated, and addressed before uncertainty becomes an unmanaged operational risk. For me, this is one of the important engineering challenges in moving AI beyond demonstrations and into production. The more autonomy we introduce, the less acceptable it becomes to treat the final output as the only evidence that matters.

We need to observe not just what the agent did, but the path from its intended action to the verified result. In blockchain applications, that path crosses probabilistic reasoning, external data, policy decisions, distributed services, and deterministic execution. Making those boundaries visible is what turns observability from a collection of dashboards into a foundation for operating autonomous systems responsibly.

The next generation of AI infrastructure will need to make these systems not only capable of acting, but also understandable when their actions do not go as planned.

#9767. Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Android device manufacturer Videostrong allegedly ran the operation, which infected set-top boxes and IoT devices with a backdoor to create infrastructure for criminal activity.

Google and industry partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, a cybercriminal operation that planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android-based set-top boxes, turning consumer devices into infrastructure for malicious activity.

The operation, attributed with "high confidence" by Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to Android device manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co., involved deliberately embedding the XCPE backdoor malware in multiple device models and brands since at least 2024, according to a blog post published earlier this week by GTIG.

Rather than simply exploiting vulnerable devices, however, the manufacturer allegedly built a system that allowed criminal affiliates to access compromised hardware and deploy their own malicious software, Google said.

"Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices," according to the post. "These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices."

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Google and its partners, which included Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI, took legal action against Videostrong to disrupt the domains and servers it used to control the botnet, install affiliate malware modules, and operate the command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used by those modules.

Because the affiliate modules "each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE," Google assessed that disrupting their C2 infrastructure "will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to the post.

Google has also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the manufacturer, along with any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. Videostrong did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment on Wednesday.

Most devices infected by the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes. However, the botnet also included other Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage systems, according to Google.

This wider exposure of IoT devices is reflected in Bitdefender's "2026 IoT Security Landscape Report," released this week. The findings recorded 5.4 billion security events and 6.2 billion vulnerability observations across devices behind approximately 10.4 million monitored routers between January and September 2026. While these figures represent detected activity and identified device vulnerabilities rather than confirmed compromises, they underline the scale of the threat facing connected devices and the potential attack surface they present to businesses.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

While most of Videostrong's interactions with victim devices involved installing, uninstalling, and configuring malware modules, operators also carried out so-called "sensitive actions," according to Google. These include capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive information, such as account and device details, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including those used to establish reverse shells on infected devices.

Although the operation primarily targeted consumer devices, it has significant security implications for businesses and enterprise organizations. XCPE demonstrates how compromised IoT equipment can be turned into criminal infrastructure, providing attackers with residential proxy networks that help conceal malicious activity, evade IP-based security controls, and facilitate fraud.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

"By turning 1.3 million devices into residential proxies, threat actors fuel the exact infrastructure used to attack high-value API endpoints," says Mark Mazur, field chief technology officer (CTO) for mobile application security firm Approov.

Because attacks launched through the botnet can originate from legitimate consumer IP addresses, standard security defenses such as geo-blocking, ASN blocking, and IP reputation filters "are practically useless against them," he says.

"They are creating infrastructure, largely based on IoT devices, that can power sophisticated credential stuffing and API abuse campaigns," Mazur adds.

The malware's ability to execute remote commands, conduct network reconnaissance, and maintain persistent access also raises concerns about connected devices deployed in corporate and healthcare environments. Digital signage, televisions, and telehealth equipment, for example, could provide attackers with an opportunity to explore networks or establish a foothold if compromised devices are connected to inadequately segmented networks. Google has not confirmed that any such activity has occurred, however.

Google requires original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to undergo a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to participate in the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong was able to evade these checks by "employing obfuscation techniques" that exploited a weakness in the review process, according to Google. The malicious code was loaded after the device's first boot, allowing it to bypass the initial security checks.

Calling Videostrong's actions "an unacceptable breach of trust," Google said it has since strengthened its review processes to protect the integrity of Android TV firmware and "better safeguard against similar activity in the future," according to the post.

As an additional protective measure, Google encouraged consumers to be wary of applications offering payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your Internet," as these could turn their set-top boxes and other IoT products into part of a residential proxy network.

"These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device's home network," according to the post.

Google also urged Android users to stick to trusted app stores, review the permissions requested by third-party VPN and proxy applications, and ensure built-in security protections such as Google Play Protect are active.

Finally, Google called on mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces, and other technology providers to continue sharing threat intelligence and implementing security best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software to prevent similar botnet operations from emerging in the future.

#9765. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

#9763. Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

An attacker could write arbitrary files and read sensitive files via images uploaded to the Rails Active Storage ImageMagick integration, possibly positioning a threat actor for lateral movement.

A critical vulnerability in Rails could send impacted Web servers off the tracks.

Rails, or Ruby on Rails, is a Web application framework built on Ruby. The framework's Active Storage component handles file uploads and can use the ImageMagick image processing suite to analyze uploaded images. Unfortunately, a flaw enables attackers to write arbitrary files to a Web server via ImageMagick.

The vulnerability (which is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9) is critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and is considered so severe because an attacker could upload a crafted image file to write arbitrary files, read sensitive files, and access secrets such as secret_key_base files, external system credentials, database passwords, and third-party tokens. These secrets could then be used for lateral movement or remote code execution into external systems.

As a GitHub advisory published by the Rails maintainers explains, "A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process."

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

The vulnerability exists because ImageMagick doesn't necessarily decide how to process a file (i.e., which coder it uses) based on the filename or extension, but rather on its contents. This means an attacker can upload an image file named "maliciousfile.jpeg" that contains content that causes ImageMagick to invoke a different coder. This can potentially allow arbitrary file reads or writes on the server.

Vulnerable versions of Active Storage include those 8.0 versions prior to 8.0.5.2 and 8.1 versions prior to 8.1.4.1. Those affected organizations running Rails applications that use ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing run with a security policy that does not block the affected coders, and accept uploads from untrusted users.

Active Storage patches are available now. The GitHub page includes further mitigation requirements for applications that use MiniMagick and ImageMagick.

Additionally, if an application stores attachments through the Disk service, users should "change secret_key_base and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens," the GitHub advisory said. Users should not retain exposed secrets as a fallback.

If a user requires a workaround, the GitHub page offers system rules the user can apply into ImageMagick's system policy.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for exposure management vendor watchTowr, tells Dark Reading the firm has already reproduced the vulnerability in a lab environment, and "that against the right target, exploitation won't be difficult at all."

Moreover, he says he'd be surprised if public proof-of-concept exploit code took more than a few days to come to light.

"For attackers, reproducing the vulnerability here is likely the easy part, as the patterns and primitives involved in exploitation are well established," Knott says. "The hard part is finding software and deployments that are common enough, and configured in a vulnerable way, to deliver impact at scale indiscriminately."
