InfoQ Homepage News AWS Launches TorchNeuron to Run PyTorch Models on AWS Trainium Without Modifications

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

At the recent PyTorch Conference North America 2026, Amazon introduced TorchNeuron, a native PyTorch backend that enables developers to run existing PyTorch code on AWS Trainium AI chips with virtually no code modifications.

Beyond reducing engineering effort, TorchNeuron allows enterprises to share hardware capacity between training and inference workloads, reallocating resources from inference to training during off-peak hours.

Amazon says that a single configuration change is sufficient to switch hardware, eliminating the need to rewrite and revalidate models when moving to Trainium.

Today, 85% of AI researchers and developers write their code in PyTorch. Until now, the hardware that code could run on was far more limited than the code itself, and expanding to new chips meant rewriting and revalidating work that took months to perfect.

According to the TorchNeuron documentations, when leveraging PyTorch's automatic device detection through torch.accelerator, the only required change is replacing .to('cuda') to .to('neuron'). The backend also natively supports distributed training and PyTorch parallelism APIs, including DDP, FSDP2, DTensor, and others. In addition, TorchNeuron provides native support for Torch streams and events through torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event.

Amazon Annapurna Labs vice president Colin Brace, who leads the team behind TorchNeuron, emphasized that his team validated the 100,000 most popular models and more than 800 ML architectures to ensure a smooth developer experience when adopting the new backend.

Additionally, TorchNeuron enables developers and researchers to use the Neuron Kernel Interface to develop, optimize, and execute custom operators:

Developers can obtain finer performance control beyond Adaptive Eager and torch.compile by calling performance critical NKI kernels directly in model code to replace sequences of standard PyTorch operations (ATen ops).

Commenting on Amazon's announcement on LinkedId, Liner Notes Consulting CEO Yasuo Maeda noted that:

The real test will be whether developers can achieve competitive performance and total cost of ownership in production. The AI infrastructure race is not just about who builds the best chips. It is also about who makes them easiest to use at scale.

Similarly, user Pratham pratham hightlighted that, while reducing migration friction is important to avoiding accelerator lock-in, the real test lies in workload-specific performance, cost per token, and reproducibility.

Amazon also emphasizes that TorchNeuron has already been adopted by several organizations, including Cartesia, which is using it for voice AI inference, and the Lieber Institute for Brain Development, which explores applications in drug target identification and drug discovery.

AWS TorchNeuron announcement comes on the heels of Google's launch of TorchTPU, its native PyTorch backend for Google's TPU hardware.

#9760. Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Keep the three repositories side by side:

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:

After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:

The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md, then serve it with vLLM.

From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

#9759. SecurityDataPipeline.com Launches as a New Educational Resource for the AI Era

The ungated resource explains how security data pipelines reduce SIEM ingestion costs, preserve detection coverage, and prepare the data layer for AI-driven security operations.

BOSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Realm Security today launched SecurityDataPipeline.com, a new educational resource designed to help cybersecurity professionals understand security data pipelines and reduce SIEM costs without weakening detection coverage.

For many security teams, rising data volumes present a difficult choice between cutting data and keeping detections. Security data pipelines offer a way to address this challenge. Because they sit between security data sources and destinations, these platforms collect, process, filter, and route telemetry before it reaches a SIEM, data lake, or other security tool.

"Most security teams are being asked to cut SIEM spend and roll out AI agents at the same time, and both of those decisions come down to the data layer," said Chris O'Brien, VP of Marketing at Realm Security. "We built SecurityDataPipeline.com so practitioners can understand how pipelines work and how to reduce volume without losing detections, before they ever talk to a vendor, including us."

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

Security data pipelines are becoming essential infrastructure as AI reshapes the SOC. As enterprises deploy AI agents for triage, investigation, and response, the data layer underneath those agents determines whether those agents get clean, normalized context to reason over. SecurityDataPipeline.com is a resource for security leaders trying to understand how to turn raw logs and fragmented cybersecurity data into clean, actionable intelligence for AI SOC agents and other AI cybersecurity initiatives.

The resource also covers how security data pipelines route telemetry to destinations including Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, and Databricks Delta Lake; how OCSF-normalized data supports AI SOC agents; and how MITRE ATT&CK coverage can be preserved as teams reduce SIEM ingestion volumes.

On SecurityDataPipeline.com, visitors can:

Explore a beginner's guide explaining security data pipelines and their core functions.

Try an ungated interactive pipeline demonstration showing how security events are filtered, transformed, enriched, and routed.

Use a SIEM cost calculator estimating potential reductions in data ingestion costs.

Learn about practical use cases covering SIEM cost reduction, SIEM migration, SOC efficiency, data governance, and AI readiness.

Read technology comparisons explaining the differences between security data pipelines, SIEMs, data lakes, log forwarders, and observability pipelines.

The resource addresses how to reduce the cost of managing security data without weakening detection capabilities by looking at the role of data filtering, normalization, enrichment, routing, and retention. It also shows how teams can identify which information their security detections need and which data can be stored more economically.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

The website is intended for CISOs, security architects, SOC managers, and cybersecurity professionals evaluating ways to manage growing telemetry volumes.

SecurityDataPipeline.com is available at https://securitydatapipeline.com/.

Realm Security gives security teams independent control over their telemetry before it reaches the SIEM, data lake, or AI agent. The platform understands what each source produces and what each downstream system needs, then guides teams on what to keep, archive, and route. Headquartered in Boston, Realm deploys in about a week and typically cuts SIEM ingestion costs by 50% or more. Learn more at www.realm.security.

#9757. DeepSeek's Super-Agent Moves the Attention Bottleneck From Your Feed to Your Agents

Doomscroll, technology. We benchmark newsfeeds of popular apps, rating their doomscroll percentages for societal expenditures.

Doomscroll, technology. We benchmark newsfeeds of popular apps, rating their doomscroll percentages for societal expenditures.

Doomscroll, technology. We benchmark newsfeeds of popular apps, rating their doomscroll percentages for societal expenditures.

On November 1, 2026, the DeepSeek Harness team posted a technical essay, "Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System." A day later, Jen Zhu Scott quote-posted it with one line: "This is an obituary for Attention Economy."

That is a big claim for an engineering document. The essay never mentions ad markets, feeds or scrolling. It argues about agent architecture. But its core diagnosis, that human attention, not model capability, now caps how much work agents can do in parallel, pokes at the same scarce resource the ad-funded internet has monetized for two decades. To see why the line lands, and where it overreaches, start with the layer DeepSeek is redesigning: the harness.

An agent is not a model. The shorthand that spread in early 2026 is agent = model + harness, a formula the academic literature credits to LangChain's engineering writing. The model predicts tokens. The harness turns those predictions into multi-step action: the loop that keeps calling the model, the tools it may invoke, the context and memory it sees, the permission system that decides what runs freely and what waits for approval, the orchestration of sub-agents, and the extension points (skills, plugins, MCP servers, hooks) that let the system grow without a rewrite.

A July 2026 source-code study of eleven production coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenHands, Aider and Hermes, read roughly four million lines of code and found the same seven subsystems in every one: agent loop, LLM integration, tools, memory and context, safety, orchestration and extensibility. None of them import a general-purpose agent framework, and the SKILL.md format now shows up in more of them (9 of 11) than MCP (8 of 11). The paper, Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents, closes with 18 design recommendations and a 90-line starter harness that implements ten of them. HackerNoon writers have been circling the same conclusion: agent reliability depends more on the harness than the model.

Developer NO1ennn read that paper and called harness engineering "the most f*cking DANGEROUS and accessible thing" he had ever seen. Both adjectives describe the same fact. Ninety lines buy a loop that can touch the filesystem, the terminal and the network. The model is rented or open-weight. The harness is the part you own, and the part that decides what the model may do when nobody is watching.

The scaffolding mattered before it had a name. ReAct-style reasoning loops and the 2024 SWE-agent paper showed that redesigning the agent-computer interface could move benchmark scores as much as swapping the model. Practitioners spent years building system prompts, tool schemas, permission policies and sandboxes without a shared term for the work.

The term arrived in early 2026. The Wavestone researchers behind the source-code study credit Mitchell Hashimoto with first using "harness engineering" in passing and LangChain's Vivek Trivedy with defining it. Hashimoto's version is practical: every time an agent makes a mistake, engineer a permanent fix into its environment so the mistake cannot recur. By mid-2026 the harness was an object of academic study, and DeepSeek pushed the idea to its limit with DeepSeek Harness, where even the agent loop is a plugin. There is no privileged core to patch.

NO1ennn's own long-form post shows what this looks like at night. He built the harness around his agent (context, tools, loop, evals, rules) but hated running his 412-eval suite every evening and triaging the failures. So he gave the night shift to an agent named Viktor: run the suite at 2 AM, compare failures with the night before, propose fixes as pull requests, and "do not merge or change anything on your own." Viktor prepares. A human signs. That one constraint separates a tool that runs when you run it from a system that owns a job while a person keeps signature authority.

DeepSeek Harness (dsh) is an MIT-licensed, model-agnostic agent runtime whose README sums up its design as "Everything is a Plugin": the model adapter, tool registry, session log, sandbox, scheduler, UI and the agent loop itself. It runs on the Cordis plugin framework and launches as a local web UI with a single npx command. The repo now shows more than 270,000 GitHub stars.

The November essay, written by Yujia Qiao of the Harness team, names the single session as the next bottleneck. Models now finish complex tasks with less steering, so the constraint has moved. "A single task is limited by model capability, but multi-tasking is limited by human attention," the team wrote, adding that a person can actively track only three to five concurrent sessions. Past that point, more capable agents add context-switching costs instead of output.

The proposed Super-agent has four properties: continuous, productive, proactive and persistent. It is reachable across chat apps and GitHub comments without the user tracking sessions, it runs parallel tasks, it reacts to events without being prompted, and it recovers from failures. Architecturally, a long-lived Router session handles the human conversation and dispatches isolated Worker sessions for individual tasks. DeepSeek also contrasts its approach with Anthropic's "Decoupling the brain from the hands," noting that its design must first connect personal computers that are often only intermittently online.

The team released an MIT-licensed research prototype alongside the essay. In simulated workloads, the Super-agent finished tasks at a median of 12.4 minutes versus 20.4 minutes for a single-session agent. DeepSeek calls it "only a prototype for validating the technical approach, not an official DeepSeek product."

The idea traces to Herbert Simon's 1971 observation that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. For most of history, information was scarce. Once computers, networks and mass media reversed that, attention became the binding constraint.

In the 1990s, Michael Goldhaber's Wired essay "Attention Shoppers!" turned the observation into an economic claim: attention, more than information or even money, would become the real currency of cyberspace. Goldhaber described a pure attention economy of stars and fans. The commercial internet built something narrower: ad-funded platforms engineering notifications, recommendation feeds and infinite scroll to maximize time-on-site, then selling access to that time. HackerNoon contributors have argued that focus is becoming the class divide of this century for exactly that reason.

Almost not at all. The Super-agent is a prototype released days ago. Its benchmarks use simulated workloads, not real multi-user environments. DeepSeek Harness has serious developer traction as infrastructure, but it does not compete with consumer platforms or ad markets.

The idea is landing, though, while other arguments converge on the same weak point. IEEE Spectrum reports that digital advertisers may soon compete for AI agents' attention rather than humans'. Economists have modeled an "attention lemons" problem in two-sided ad markets once agents do the browsing. California Management Review describes a "trust economy" in which agents rewrite the rules of digital strategy. And on HackerNoon, one writer argues that AI coding already created a new attention market, while another warns that multitasking across coding agents drains the attention it was meant to save.

None of this dents Meta, Google, TikTok or the open-web ad stack this week. What changed is the recognition, visible in both DeepSeek's essay and NO1ennn's night shift, that the scarce resource is no longer only the hours a person spends scrolling. It is also the hours a person spends supervising the agents that were supposed to free those hours.

The same 90-line starter that makes harness engineering accessible makes it dangerous. A model without a harness is a chat window. A model with a good harness can read private files, run shell commands, open pull requests, send messages, schedule recurring work and recover from its own failures. The Super-agent hides the session-management tax so one person can keep more of that work in flight. Open, trivial-to-start harnesses plus architectures that demand less supervision lower the barrier to deploying systems with persistence and reach.

Viktor's "do not merge or change anything on your own" is one careful answer. It is not a prompt trick but a hard boundary in the harness: every action that matters waits for a human yes. Today the person who built the harness enforces that boundary. As Super-agent-style systems grow more continuous and proactive, the open question is whether the boundary stays a deliberate engineering choice or erodes under the pressure of "just let it finish."

Accessibility also means failure modes are no longer confined to well-funded labs. Anyone who can write a SKILL.md, configure a plugin or fork a 90-line loop can hand a model real-world effectors. Safety is one of the seven canonical subsystems precisely because the other six can do damage. When the harness is the product, its bugs are capability bugs: a context window that silently drops a constraint, a tool description that is slightly too broad, a permission policy that fails open. HackerNoon's own chronicle of the period, The Age of the Lobster, catalogs how quickly those effectors spread.

The structural question is more interesting. Today's agent interfaces keep the session as the unit of work: open a chat, assign a task, watch it, switch contexts, restate goals. The human is the router. The Super-agent moves routing into the system so the person works at the level of decisions and approvals. If that pattern spreads, three things follow.

First, attention per unit of work falls. DeepSeek's team says plainly that the bottleneck to further productivity is shifting toward human attention. A continuous agent that dispatches parallel work and surfaces results only when judgment is needed attacks the assumption that more capable agents must consume proportionally more human attention.

Second, the main consumer of interfaces may change. When agents browse, compare, buy and coordinate for us, value flows to interfaces that are machine-readable and criteria-satisfying rather than sticky. Content built for emotional engagement or variable-reward notifications matters less if the agent never scrolls. Media companies will face pressure to publish material that agents can parse, trust and act on.

Third, attention gets reallocated, not abolished. Goldhaber's point was that people's appetite for attention has no upper bound. Freeing attention from low-level monitoring raises the value of what remains for high-stakes judgment, relationships and creative work. Others warn of an "intention economy", in which platforms move upstream from capturing attention to forecasting and selling intentions before users fully form them.

The counter-forces are real. Ad and recommendation systems will adapt. Platforms can still monetize the moments when humans review agent output, set goals or resolve ambiguity. Synthetic agents that mimic human engagement can pollute metrics. Coordination between agents remains harder than individual competence. The harness layer simply moves the scarce resource one level up: from the content that captures attention to the systems that decide what agents attend to on our behalf.

Platforms engineering for maximum human engagement still dominate. The prototype has not proven it scales, its tests are synthetic, and the ad infrastructure is vast. Obituaries get written after the fact. This is a design document.

It is, however, a precise diagnosis of a moving bottleneck and a concrete architectural response. "Multi-tasking is limited by human attention" names the same scarcity Simon described in 1971, now appearing inside the agent stack. If systems that route work, act proactively and need less supervision become the default interface to the digital world, the logic that rewards capturing human attention for its own sake loses force. Value moves toward systems that satisfy agent criteria, earn trust for delegated action and give attention back.

Harness engineering makes that shift more accessible and more dangerous at once. Open-source runtimes lower the cost of giving a model real effectors. The Super-agent lowers the ongoing attention cost of keeping them running. Together they move the scarce resource from "who can capture human eyes" to "who designs the boundaries that still require a human yes." NO1ennn kept the signature. Whether that stays the default or becomes a setting most people switch off is the question the next few years of harness design will answer.

InfoQ Homepage News Cloudflare Develops Public Certificate Authority for Post-Quantum Web Security

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

Cloudflare has tested Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) as an alternative to traditional certificate chains, reporting 9% faster median performance in a Chrome experiment. The approach batches certificate data into an append-only Merkle tree, letting clients verify certificates with compact inclusion proofs instead of transmitting a full certificate chain. Cloudflare attributed most of the measured improvement to eliminating intermediate certificates; the experiment used classical signatures rather than post-quantum signatures.

Building on the approach covered in InfoQ’s earlier report, Cloudflare describes how landmark-based verification and independent transparency log cosigners support certificate issuance and verification at scale.

The experiment served billions of MTCs to 50% of Chrome Beta 146 for selected domains on Cloudflare’s free plan. Cloudflare wound down the experiment in August 2026 and is developing a public certificate authority (CA) that supports MTC issuance, targeting inclusion in Chrome’s quantum-resistant Root Store in early 2027, subject to evaluation.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, in a press release, said:

Upgrading the web's security before quantum computers can break it is one of the biggest coordination challenges in the history of the Internet.

Post-quantum cryptography creates scaling challenges for the Web Public Key Infrastructure (Web PKI). According to Cloudflare, post-quantum signatures can be approximately 40 times larger than classical signatures, increasing bandwidth and storage requirements.

MTCs combine certificate issuance with transparency logging. Instead of signing certificates individually, a certificate authority (CA) records certificate data in an append-only Merkle tree and signs a checkpoint. Clients verify certificate inclusion using cryptographic proofs.

Cloudflare uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol to validate domain ownership. An independent mirroring cosigner verifies and stores updated tree states, helping detect inconsistent log views and preserve issuance records if the original log becomes unavailable.

MTC issuance and independent log mirroring (Source: Cloudflare Blog Post)

Landmark relative certificates further reduce TLS handshake data. Cloudflare distributes authenticated landmarks to clients, which verify certificate inclusion using cryptographic proofs. Servers must still prove possession of their private keys. In the common case, the handshake transmits one public key, one signature, and an inclusion proof smaller than 1 KB.

Landmark relative certificate verification using pre-distributed tree landmarks. (Source: Cloudflare Blog Post)

Clients may be newly installed, offline, or missing the relevant landmark update. Servers must therefore retain a standalone MTC certificate as a fallback. Cloudflare identifies independent monitoring at production volume, a diverse ecosystem of CAs and cosigners, and browser support as remaining requirements for broader deployment. Alicja Tendaj, Tier 2 Technical Support Specialist at SSL.com, raised questions about revocation and incident handling in response to Cloudflare’s announcement on LinkedIn:

With short validity and trust anchored in a tree head, a lot of the old OCSP and CRL playbook becomes a question of how quickly you can stop including a certificate

Cloudflare’s planned public CA will require evaluation before its MTC issuance can be trusted through Chrome’s quantum-resistant Root Store. The company says production deployment will help determine whether the approach can maintain transparency, interoperability, and availability at Internet scale.

#9754. APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

After compromising websites, the Russian state-sponsored threat group is fingerprinting victims, then harvesting information from the interesting ones.

It has emerged this week that Russia's APT29 threat group compromised the website of a Ukrainian SEO and website analytics service, and briefly used the access to distribute malicious device-fingerprinting code to potentially thousands of iPhone and Android users.

The weeklong compromise earlier this year was part of a broader watering-hole campaign from APT29 (aka Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes) that also used other legitimate and fake websites to distribute the fingerprinting malware, and later to collect sensitive personal information from selected devices.

Researchers at Sekoia who are tracking the campaign are unsure if the state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) had specific targets in mind, or if it was simply trying to infect as many vulnerable phones as possible.

"Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis," Sekoia's threat research and intelligence team wrote. "While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation."

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

APT29 is a familiar threat actor that the US government has formally tied to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its primary mission is intelligence gathering on behalf of Moscow, with a focus on government agencies, diplomatic organizations, think tanks, technology companies, healthcare, and research institutions.

Among its most prominent campaigns were the breaches at the Democratic National Committee in 2016, efforts to steal COVID-19 vaccine research in 2020, and the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, which gave it access to numerous US government agencies and private-sector organizations. The group is known for stealthy, long-term intrusions, and in recent years has increasingly targeted cloud environments, email accounts, and technology providers to gain access to downstream victims.

In its latest campaign, APT29 used three separate infection vectors to target iOS and Android devices. One involved compromising legitimate websites and injecting malicious JavaScript that exposed visitors to a device-fingerprinting script. Among the websites the threat actor turned into watering holes were those of a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, and a Bulgarian military-related organization.

When unable to compromise a legitimate website, the group created lookalike domains that impersonated the real sites, and modified their content in real-time to inject the malicious code. Two examples it impersonated were the America250 national celebration website and London's Raffles hotel.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

The third vector involved a supply chain compromise of Ukrainian website analytics firm Plerdy. According to Sekoia, thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, use the company's tracking scripts. By injecting malicious code into that script, APT29 potentially exposed visitors to those sites to its device-fingerprinting and exploit-delivery infrastructure, Sekoia said.

The fingerprinting malware collected device and browser data from Android and iOS devices and sent it to an APT29 command-and-control service, which then delivered one of three different exploit chains depending on the mobile platform and browser/OS versions. Each chain targeted specific vulnerabilities in iOS or Android that had remained unpatched on the exposed devices.

Related:Video Call Exploit Chains Two Flaws in Unisoc Modems

Sekoia said it found several indicators linking the campaign to APT29, including remnants of a separate 2025 watering-hole operation that researchers have previously attributed to the group. Sekoia also found signs that the attackers may have obtained their exploits from a third party, possibly a commercial surveillance vendor (CSV). The campaign's victims include organizations in Europe and the US, though most are based in Ukraine, a country that Russian threat groups have incessantly targeted since the beginning of the war in Ukraine.

APT29's latest campaign is another indication of how mobile devices have become attractive intelligence targets for threat groups. Commercial spyware vendors are fueling the trend by making technology available that enables large scale surveillance and data theft via mobile devices. APT29's likely sourcing of the DarkSword exploit kit from a third-party provider suggests that sophisticated mobile intrusion capabilities that were once largely associated with highly targeted espionage operations are finding their way into broader campaigns.

"The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation," Sekoia warned. "Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9753. Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#9752. What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from an ill-conceived phishing simulation to a hacktivist attack on a US government agency.

Phishing tests can be an important part of cybersecurity awareness training. But as the NBA champion New York Knicks recently showed, they can also go awry.

According to a recent report in The Athletic, Madison Square Garden (MSG) Sports, which owns the Knicks, deployed a poorly timed and ill-conceived phishing simulation ahead of its banner-raising ceremony on Oct. 20. MSG Sports sent out emails to employees with offers of free championship rings commemorating the team's historic NBA Finals victory in June.

Team employees often receive championship rings at the start of the following season. However, the emails in this case were part of a phishing simulation, and when employees clicked on the links to select their rings, they were informed they failed the test and had to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. And they didn't get the rings, either.

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: a hacktivist group breached the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and published personnel records for more than 40,000 employees, and it's unclear how the agency was compromised; and a New York Times report claims a NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles; and, sign up for the Dark Reading newsletter!

DR's Rob Wright: So there's that. There's physical security concerns here with infiltration of foreign agents, foreign assets trying to get in, steal trade secrets, steal intelligence, steal policy, developing policy moves and get ahead of them, etc.

I think the thing that's interesting here is that I know NVIDIA came out and said, this is normal. Like, he meets with a lot of CEOs and stuff like that. And there's nothing salacious in this story. It doesn't say that they had a romantic relationship or like intimate relationship of any kind. It just says close relationship.

But to me, if I were them — if I were NVIDIA, and if I were the US government — I would try to come out with a little bit more information about this to qualify, you know, what steps were taken to warn him, what steps were taken to, if any, to get ahead of this, to mitigate the threat, and to move away from this person who's been identified as a Chinese asset. And there really isn't a lot of information in the story about what they did to address it. So I think that's a little concerning, like they maybe are not totally up for the challenge here of dealing with foreign tradecraft, spy craft here. And they should, because they should know that they're a target, to your point. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, like everyone is a target now for in the AI industry for this stuff. This is an arms race. Plain and simple.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yeah, and social engineering remains robust, well-fortified, integral, vital to the hacker ecosystem. No matter what technologies get introduced, the only thing it seems to do is make social engineering more powerful. Maybe that's kind of a running trend, at least with the first and third stories we talk about this week.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, for real. Yeah. Interesting week of stories. But that's it for this episode of "What We Missed." Thanks, Alex. I appreciate the time.

#9751. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9750. ODF vs. Managed Block Storage on IBM Cloud: How I Model the Tradeoff for Stateful Workloads

Product Manager, IBM Cloud PaaS, Containers Solutions

Product Manager, IBM Cloud PaaS, Containers Solutions

Product Manager, IBM Cloud PaaS, Containers Solutions

The old myth that "containers are only for stateless workloads" died years ago. Today, production Kubernetes environments routinely host mission-critical stateful workloads, from transactional databases and Kafka clusters to AI/ML feature stores and virtual machines.

When teams move stateful applications into production on Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Cloud, they quickly encounter a fundamental storage architecture decision: Should they use cloud-managed block volumes, or deploy in-cluster software-defined storage with OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF)?

Treating storage like an afterthought works fine until a database pod restarts on a new node and sits in CrashLoopBackOff while you explain to leadership what an attach-detach timeout is. As the product manager working on container storage at IBM Cloud, I walk engineering teams through this choice every week. Both storage architectures are mature, production-proven options, but they optimize for fundamentally different operational priorities.

To make the right choice, you first have to understand where the storage intelligence lives in each model.

IBM Cloud Block Storage operates outside your Kubernetes compute nodes. When a stateful pod requests a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC), the IBM Cloud Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver calls the VPC storage API to provision a dedicated, NVMe-backed volume on the cloud storage fabric and attaches it directly to the host hypervisor.

OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) takes the opposite approach. Powered by open-source Ceph, Rook, and NooBaa, ODF aggregates the physical NVMe drives attached to your bare-metal worker nodes into a single, unified, software-defined storage pool managed by Kubernetes operators.

The most immediate technical differentiator between these two storage models comes down to access modes and application architecture.

For standard database engines running in high availability (such as a PostgreSQL or MySQL StatefulSet with a primary and read-replicas), each replica manages its own dedicated storage volume. Replica synchronization happens at the application database layer rather than the storage layer.

For these workloads, IBM Cloud Block Storage using the ibmc-vpc-block-10iops-tier or dynamic Storage Defined Performance (SDP) profile is exceptional. You get guaranteed IOPS, volume snapshots, and online capacity expansion without running storage daemons on your nodes.

Traditional cloud-managed block volumes are exposed as single-attached ReadWriteOnce (RWO) storage through Kubernetes, making them unsuitable for workloads that require simultaneous multi-node access. If your workload requires concurrent writes from multiple pods (such as shared data ingestion pipelines, machine learning training sets, or CMS asset pools), ODF provides native POSIX-compliant CephFS with ReadWriteMany (RWX) access across all nodes.

Even more critical is Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization. When running virtual machines on OpenShift alongside containers, migrating running VMs across physical hosts without downtime (the cloud-native equivalent of VMware vMotion) requires shared-access storage.

Standard cloud block storage cannot support live migration because the hypervisor on the destination node cannot attach a volume that is still locked to the source node. OpenShift Virtualization addresses this by consuming Ceph RBD in raw block mode (volumeMode: Block) rather than as a mounted filesystem. ODF provides validated storage classes like ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization with shared access patterns. Destination nodes mount the disk image before migration begins, transferring memory states with zero guest downtime.

Engineering is always a study in tradeoffs. ODF is powerful, but deploying it blindly for every workload is a major architectural mistake.

ODF requires bare-metal worker nodes with local NVMe drives. The absolute architectural minimum is 3 worker nodes, with 6 nodes recommended for production clusters so you can drain a node for maintenance without degrading replication.

If you are running a small cluster with 3 Virtual Server Instances (VSIs) hosting a few microservices and a lightweight cache, spinning up 3 or 6 bare-metal nodes just to run Ceph makes zero financial sense. Managed VPC Block allows you to run small, flexible VSI instances and attach 20 GB or 100 GB volumes on demand.

Because ODF uses a default replica factor of 3 for high availability, 30 TB of raw NVMe storage yields roughly 10 TB of usable application capacity. Additionally, Ceph OSDs, Monitors, and Metadata Servers run as pods inside your cluster, consuming worker node memory and CPU cycles.

In Ceph, you must actively govern capacity. When an ODF cluster reaches ~80% capacity (nearfull), Ceph begins throttling write operations to prevent disk starvation. At ~85% capacity (full), Ceph blocks new writes entirely to protect cluster consistency. (Ceph is fantastic, but when it hits 85% full and starts refusing writes to protect data integrity, it will definitely get your team's undivided attention.)

With managed VPC Block, each volume is completely isolated. If volume A fills up, volume B is unaffected, and you can resize any attached volume online with a single pvc spec update.

ODF embeds a full distributed storage system inside your cluster. Even though IBM Cloud automates deployment and day-2 operator lifecycle management on ROKS, platform teams must still understand cluster storage health, data rebalancing behavior during node maintenance, and proactive capacity planning.

When evaluating storage for your stateful workloads on IBM Cloud, use this comparison framework:

If you answer yes to any of these questions, evaluate OpenShift Data Foundation:

If you answered no to all of the above, start with IBM Cloud Block Storage—it gives you lightweight, fully isolated, pay-as-you-go persistence with zero storage cluster operational overhead.

On generic cloud setups or DIY Kubernetes, operating Ceph is notoriously complex. Cluster operators often spend days configuring CRUSH maps, tuning OSD placement, and managing daemon recovery during node upgrades.

This is where the platform architecture matters. On competing hyperscaler Kubernetes platforms (such as AKS, EKS, or GKE), ODF is not generally available as a native managed platform add-on. On ROSA and ARO, customers must manually install and maintain ODF operators.

On Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Cloud (ROKS), ODF is delivered as a fully managed IBM Cloud add-on. IBM SREs handle operator deployment, daemon lifecycle, health monitoring, and version patching, allowing platform teams to consume Ceph storage classes directly via standard Kubernetes manifests without operating the underlying storage infrastructure.

Choose IBM Cloud Block Storage when you want lightweight, pay-as-you-go, isolated block volumes for databases running on flexible virtual server instances with zero storage daemon overhead.

Choose OpenShift Data Foundation when you run bare-metal OpenShift clusters that demand high-throughput local NVMe performance, multi-modal storage consolidation (block + file + object), or live migration for OpenShift Virtualization VMs.

How does your team model the line between cloud-managed storage volumes and software-defined in-cluster storage for your Kubernetes clusters?

InfoQ Homepage News Google Releases Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics Control, Simulation, and Policy Improvement

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

Google has released Gemini 4 Argon framing it as a general-purpose physical-reasoning model for robot control, Real2Sim scene construction, multimodal labeling of robot video, and iterative policy improvement, rather than as a single end-effector policy.

In the published prompts, Argon directs a Boston Dynamics Spot through a foot-pedal task after practice in a MuJoCo twin, steers a simpler arm with visual coordinates and HTTP motion primitives, and closes a loop with the Gemini Omni video world model. Real2Sim examples rebuild MuJoCo scenes from teleoperation video; labeling prompts annotate demonstration footage for behavior cloning. Google also reports synthesizing domain-randomized MuJoCo episodes from one RGB photo to fine-tune a vision-language-action policy, citing a rise from 56% to 75% success on the corresponding real setup.

Early practitioner reaction focused on simulation fidelity. Davin YC Dong commented on X:

Google's Argon robotics examples tune simulation twins against contact events as well as visuals. That is the part I'd inspect: a scene can look convincing while its objects behave incorrectly. For manipulation, matching what happens at contact matters as much as matching pixels.

Separately, a developer posting as pulpmatrix argued for source discipline around Video-to-Sim-to-Real claims circulating the same week:

Video-to-Sim-to-Real is real, documented in Google's Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics dev blog (MuJoCo twin, 87% ERQA). Cornhole isn't in it: no paper, no repo, no hit rate, and real throws calibrated the robot first.

Specialized vision-language-action systems such as OpenVLA-class policies, Physical Intelligence's π-family models, and NVIDIA GR00T with Isaac-oriented tooling optimize for action prediction under robot embodiments and typically rely on large teleoperation or simulation corpora. Scene-to-sim and generative world tools, World Labs-style reconstructions, NVIDIA DreamDojo-style action video, and Isaac Sim digital twins, emphasize environment synthesis or video prediction without necessarily owning the full control-and-QC loop shown in Google's prompts. Prior Google work such as Gemini Robotics-ER remains a related line for spatial perception and planning. For architecture reviews, the question is whether one frontier model plus heavy prompt harnesses displaces a pipeline of VLA, simulator, and labeler services.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness
