#9738. Dutch Police Arrest ‘Reformed’ Hacker in Shiny Hunters Investigation

Authorities in the Netherlands have arrested a 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by the prolific hacker group ShinyHunters. In the days immediately following the suspect’s arrest, remaining ShinyHunters members dramatically escalated their attacks, stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the Russian ransomware group Cl0p.

According to three sources familiar with the matter, the Dutch man arrested by authorities this month is Pepijn van der Stap, a convicted cybercriminal from Almere and Lelystad in the Netherlands. Van der Stap was previously convicted in 2023 in connection with a string of data thefts and extortions that prosecutors said earned between €1.5 million and €2.7 million.

At his trial in late 2023, van der Stap admitted that he lived a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde existence, secretly using the hacker handle “Umbreon” to extort victims and post their data on English language hacking communities like the now-defunct RaidForums and Breached. By day, however, van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD), a nonprofit security research group.

Pepijn van der Stap’s alter ego “Umbreon” selling a database on RaidForums, offering information on 2.3 million people from The Netherlands in September 2021. This user’s avatar is a depiction of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: KELA.

Van der Stap confessed to his data theft and extortion activity, and was sentenced to four years in prison (one of which was suspended). During his trial, van der Stap opted to remain in custody for a time rather than at home, saying he could not find better treatment on the outside for his ongoing psychological issues, which he claimed included PTSD related to childhood trauma. He was released from prison in December 2025.

In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, 2026, Van der Stap cast himself as a reformed hacker who was trying to turn his life around and make a positive contribution to society. Van der Stap is currently employed as offensive security lead at the Dutch company Neo Security, which did not respond to requests for comment.

Van der Stap said he was still dealing with civil lawsuits and restitution related to his previous cybercrime victims, and that he was trying his best to make amends. But not long after that interview, the Dutch hacker abruptly stopped replying to messages. Efforts by others close to him also repeatedly failed to elicit a response for the past two weeks.

The LinkedIn profile for Pepijn van der Stap.

According to two sources with knowledge of the matter, Van der Stap was arrested by Dutch authorities on or around September 16, and has been held in custody for questioning since. One source said a colleague of theirs personally witnessed Dutch authorities carting items out of Van der Stap’s residence.

Authorities in the Netherlands have been asking the public for help in identifying the voice in a recorded telephone call from February 2026 in which a native Dutch-speaking ShinyHunters member social engineered their way into Odido, the nation’s largest mobile telecommunications provider. In that intrusion, ShinyHunters tricked an Odido employee into logging in at a spoofed website, and then used that access to steal data on more than 6.2 million Dutch people.

Responding to Dutch news media, ShinyHunters confirmed that the suspect in the audio clip is indeed a member of the hacker collective.

“Our team member has our full support – emotionally, mentally, and financially,” the hackers said. “Everything has been arranged, including a criminal defense lawyer. We do not look down on our staff and members; we take excellent care of them,” reads a statement ShinyHunters shared with NL Times. It remains unclear if the Dutch police have matched the Odido caller to a confirmed real-life identity. The Dutch police unit handling the Odido incident did not respond to requests for comment.

The group also lashed out at the authorities in the Netherlands. “The Dutch police will need all the luck in the world – and everyone’s prayers – if they want to catch him before we carry out another large-scale data theft in the Netherlands,” the ShinyHunters statement said. “Frankly, the Dutch police are a big joke; they are incapable of doing anything. Incompetent. Irrelevant. Unimportant. Useless.”

Just days after sources say Van der Stap was detained by Dutch authorities, ShinyHunters claimed credit for an unusually brazen breach at the FBI’s job application site apply.fbijobs.gov. According to reporting from 404 Media, the data stolen from the FBI site includes Social Security numbers and personal information on more than 5,000 officials.

404 Media and Reuters reported the FBI data included each person’s job title or team, such as special agent, threat intake examiner, major cybercrimes unit, and those investigating cyber threats from foreign state-backed actors. Reuters examined documents shared by ShinyHunters and found they included sensitive psychiatric and medical files of FBI staff. The FBI issued a brief statement confirming the hack.

ShinyHunters said it gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a recently patched vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the software giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for the Peoplesoft vulnerability that ShinyHunters reportedly began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations who couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

But on Friday, BleepingComputer reported that ShinyHunters used a URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules designed to mitigate the threat from the PeopleSoft flaw. In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Van der Stap’s former hacker alias Umbreon was hidden in plain sight throughout the imagery ShinyHunters used to spread news about the FBI hack: The defacement image that ShinyHunters left behind on the hacked FBI jobs site included an ASCII art design featuring the Pokemon character Umbreon. The message at the top read, “This site has been seized by ShinyHunters. rooting your systems since ’19 ;)” The image appears identical to a defacement message ShinyHunters used in their 2020 hack of the English-language cybercrime community Hackforums.

The defacement message left by ShinyHunters on the FBI jobs site included an ASCII art rendition of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: Bleeping Computer.

Multiple sources close to the ShinyHunters investigation said the group’s recent risky attacks against the FBI and one of Russia’s most venerated ransomware groups amounted to a major pivot away from the more measured tenor of the hacking gang’s operations. Those sources said the sudden shift came about after ShinyHunters was taken over by a teenage cybercriminal from Amman, Jordan who goes by the nickname Rey and operates as part of a cybercrime group called ScatteredLapsussHunters (SLSH), which experts say is an amalgamation of three hacking groups — Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$ and ShinyHunters.

Those sources said Rey had an ongoing beef with the Dutch hacker over control of the ShinyHunters brand and data, and that the inclusion of the oversized Umbreon Pokemon image in the FBI jobs site defacement was likely an attempt by Rey to pin the hack on the Dutchman.

Rey was first publicly identified by the cybersecurity firm KELA in March 2025. In advance of our November 2025 profile of Rey, KrebsOnSecurity messaged Rey’s father and asked for permission to interview his teenage son. Rey’s dad merely forwarded the message to his son, who admitted to participating in ransomware attacks and said he was trying to extricate himself from the SLSH hacker group.

Immediately after news of the FBI jobs site hack was picked up in the media, Rey’s main account on Twitter/X (Ryan Moran/@rmoskovy) was taunting the Cl0p ransomware group and the FBI, crudely depicting them as the twin towers in New York being struck by planes labeled “cl0p drama” and “fbi breach claim.” In the foreground of the city is the giant Pokemon figure of Umbreon.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey’s now-defunct account on Sept. 22. A giant float-sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

On Sept. 24, KrebsOnSecurity again contacted Rey’s dad, asking to interview him and his son for a story on Rey’s apparent ascendency as the head of ShinyHunters. Just hours after that request, Rey deleted his longtime Twitter/X account. Meanwhile, Rey’s dad, who works for the Royal Jordanian Airlines, has failed to respond to a half-dozen emailed requests for comment about his son’s alleged activities.

Where does the bad blood between SLSH and ShinyHunters come from? According to a story in Wired this month, ShinyHunters and SLSH members briefly partnered earlier this year to help better monetize important stolen credentials collected by TeamPCP, an upstart group that was having great success compromising global code supply chains with malicious software but hadn’t been able to profit much from their stolen data (two alleged leaders of TeamPCP were arrested last month in Australia, and in an interview the TeamPCP leader claimed they made just $20,000).

The Wired story noted how Mandiant had infiltrated TeamPCP and was secretly responsible for having the crime group’s stolen credentials burned so quickly: Mandiant was secretly feeding those credentials to the major cloud providers like Amazon and Microsoft, who quickly invalidated the stolen keys. Meanwhile, the formerly cooperating hacker groups began to blame one another for causing the credentials to become worthless.

Wired’s Andy Greenberg reported that a few weeks after partnering with TeamPCP, “ShinyHunters went rogue, carrying out its own extortions with TeamPCP’s credentials but without giving the supply-chain hackers their cut.”

Mandiant researcher Austin Larsen told KrebsOnSecurity earlier this month that ShinyHunters has been enjoying a successful extortion spree so far this year, and is on track to pull in nearly $100 million in extortion payments from cybercrime victims in 2026.

Van der Stap claims he was never motivated by money and that his earlier hacker activity was driven by a desire to have the world’s most complete collection of stolen databases. Speaking with reporters from Bloomberg in 2024, Van der Stap said that singular focus in turn fueled his desire to carry out cyberattacks.

“The hacking was very easy for me, and it wasn’t a compulsion,” he told Bloomberg. “My habit was collecting. Collecting data, organizing data, downloading data, creating folders.”

DIVD, the nonprofit security research group where Van der Stap previously served as a volunteer, disclosed on LinkedIn last week that the organization was dealing with an internal cybersecurity incident that appears to have involved the malicious use of artificial intelligence. DIVD has released few details about that incident, but a spokesperson for the nonprofit told KrebsOnSecurity it does not appear related to ShinyHunters, nor are there any signs the matter involves the work of a previous volunteer.

Update: 3:44 p.m. ET: Corrected Van der Stap’s age, which is 24 (not 23).

Update, 4:54 p.m. ET: The Dutch police have confirmed the arrest of a 24-year-old in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. In a statement on Twitter/X, the Dutch police said the man will appear on Tuesday, September 29 before the chambers of the Rotterdam District Court, and that it will provide more information tomorrow.

Sept. 29, 9:42 a.m. ET: The Dutch news outlet RTL reports that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. RTL reported the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications the suspect gave the order for this.

The FBI released a short video message on the ShinyHunters investigation from Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI’s cyber division, who thanked Dutch law enforcement partners for their assistance and urged remaining ShinyHunters members to turn themselves in.

“Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk, and seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who’s left,” Leatherman said. “The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us, and we know how to find you. I suggest you reach out to us while the choice is still yours.”

The detail that keeps sticking with me is van der Stap volunteering at DIVD while living a double life — it really shows how ‘reformed’ can be a performance when the skills are that transferable. The voice identification angle is fascinating too: Dutch authorities asking the public to help identify the Odido caller’s voice is an unusual investigative tactic for a telecom intrusion.

One question I keep coming back to: with Rey and the SLSH crew openly beefing with ShinyHunters, how much of this takedown momentum is coming from infighting rather than investigative breakthroughs? Fascinating reporting as always.

It never ceases to amaze how often the same damn exact two ‘low-level’ “hacker forums” have been involved in exactly this. It is almost like hacking that one forum, in fact, is a dramatic rite of passage in the ‘busted’ certification path.

The use of the Umbreon imagery after Van der Stap’s arrest is particularly intriguing. If rival hackers were deliberately trying to frame or taunt him, it shows how difficult attribution becomes when cybercrime groups are simultaneously attacking targets and manipulating the public narrative around those attacks.

All that Pokemon stuff is just incredibly stupid peacocking.

The PeopleSoft angle is especially interesting. ShinyHunters reportedly bypassing Mandiant’s web application firewall rules with URL encoding shows why temporary mitigations can age badly once attackers start adapting. The Dutch arrest may be the headline, but the exploitation details are probably the more useful lesson for defenders.

That they used an exploitation technique that is about two decades old (a not-0day plus an url encoding trick?)

It seems to me the lesson is merely that if you throw enough spaghetti at a wall most of the spaghetti will fall off and a few noodles will go to prison; the rest of the pot apparently then can just go on and exploit. The drama just picks the cases for the feds.

Imagine 10 years down the line, this guy gets his life together, and this article still exists. This is why some voices are all in favor of SOME censorship.

What a crazy organization to just openly exist. It’s just using the “no soldier left behind” recruitment strategy in broad daylight. Wild.

#9737. UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The UK is betting on domestic AI and cyber investment to reduce reliance on US tech — but security leaders question whether the funding is too fragmented and too late.

The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools. In late October, the government unveiled a funding package of approximately $800 million to strengthen cyber defenses and AI security investments.

The move comes as Kanishka Narayan, the UK's minister of artificial intelligence, said in a speech last month that "it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber-defenses will be breached." He cited the recent trend of misaligned models escaping containment, citing the OpenAI incident in June during which an agent hacked an Australian government health agency.

But the UK government is also pushing toward another, related goal: digital sovereignty. In his speech, Narayan emphasized the need to "build in Britain to keep the public safe in Britain" and become less dependent on foreign providers, which has become a common goal for some countries following the US government's export control order for Anthropic earlier this year.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

"We want the world's leading companies investing here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment," Narayan said.

But industry-watchers argue that government investment to strengthen cyber-defenses while also achieving greater sovereignty by encouraging homegrown tech might be difficult to do all at once.

Two turning points appear to have shifted government policy in the UK and Europe this year, both involving the same US company: Anthropic. The first came with the AI company's unveiling of Project Glasswing in April for its Mythos frontier model, which sparked concerns about a coming "vulnpocalypse" for enterprise security teams.

"It created an almighty whirlpool of conversations," says Tim Williams, CEO of London-based Quod Orbis, which specializes in continuous controls monitoring. "And then there were lots of concerns about what that meant, and everybody seemed to panic. I think that panic has settled down now."

But another event — the Trump administration's ban on foreign nationals using Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models has had a far more lasting effect. The ban didn't just impact overseas companies and government agencies; the export controls effectively forced Anthropic to pull all access to the two models for several weeks.

The implications of abruptly losing access to valuable — and perhaps critical — AI technology through a sudden change in US policy accelerated an already growing conversation about reducing dependency on American tech companies. A crucial part of the UK government's funding package is designed to fuel British AI startups and invest in home-grown companies.

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

It's a solid idea, but infosec professionals see two issues with that approach. First, the funding package is split up between a number of initiatives, with approximately £154 million of the £600 million total devoted to strengthening current cyber-defenses, for example.

"If you look at the amount that they're putting into it, is that enough? Is that significant?" Williams asks.

Secondly, the UK is already well behind the curve with fueling homegrown AI and cloud companies. Amir Khan, managing director at Wire, tells Dark Reading that there's been chronic under-investment in emerging technologies in the country, which has led to missed opportunities in the past.

"In the UK, we had DeepMind before it was sold to Google [in 2014]," Khan says. "Had they known the impact that DeepMind would have now, would they still have sold it, or doubled down on it? Who knows? But it's another example of a large organization that grew in the UK, leaving to go to the US."

In fact, due to that kind of ongoing tech emigration, Khan says you could argue that the last good thing to come out of the UK's technology industry was Cambridge Analytica — a company that became embroiled in a scandal involving Facebook.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

Time and again, experts have argued that organizations can't counter AI-driven threats effectively without AI-enabled defenses. But that complicates matters for the UK, which is looking to achieve tech sovereignty in the aftermath of the Anthropic ban.

For one, in some part because of the issues outlined above, many of the major AI companies — OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence), and Palantir Technologies — are also based in the US. And while there are plenty of AI startups these days, those companies may not have the scale needed for national defense systems.

Additionally, there's also the cost component. Williams says many of Quod Orbis' customers are looking to reduce their dependency on a single vendor or provider, whether it's for cloud, software, AI, or other technologies. "There's no question that, in speaking to our clients, that concentrated risk is a concern for them," he says.

But moving from, for example, one cloud provider to four or five can be challenging, especially for mid-market organizations, he says. They may not have the budgets of large enterprises, and they probably rely more heavily on the commercial discounts that the cloud giants like AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud Platform provide. "If they're spreading that investment out across multiple cloud providers, that can become more expensive for them," Williams says.

Khan agrees and points to the recent example of France migrating off Windows for government workstations and moving to Linux. But leaving the Microsoft ecosystem will require France to add several more technologies from different vendors. "That, for me, defeats the purpose because you've essentially taken away one provider and pulled in six," he says. "That doesn't really give you the flexibility you want."

Khan argues the UK sometimes sets the wrong target for tech sovereignty. "We talk as though we have to build every chip, every cloud, and every application ourselves," he says. "As you can imagine, that's an enormous undertaking, and it doesn't really get to the heart of the issue. For me, the questions are, can we make our own decisions about the technology that we depend on? Can we operate it on our terms?"

The UK can retain such operational authority, he says, by choosing providers and vendors that build that kind of customer controls directly into their products and services; for example, Khan notes that Wire offers customers a private cloud option for the messaging platform that organizations can control and operate based within whatever country they're located.

Whichever providers or vendors the UK government chooses, officials should be asking several key questions before investing: who holds the encryption keys, who can interrupt the service, and how realistic is it to move off that technology?

In the meantime, the UK government will continue to focus on strengthening the country's cyber defenses through these investments and efforts like the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill currently. But Williams is unsure if they will be enough.

"It's a step in the right direction, absolutely," he says. "But is it the investment I would expect to see in terms of being really concerned about the threat to the UK?"

Rob Wright is a longtime reporter with more than 25 years of experience as a technology journalist. Prior to joining Dark Reading as senior news director, he spent more than a decade at TechTarget's SearchSecurity in various roles, including senior news director, executive editor and editorial director. Before that, he worked for several years at CRN, Tom's Hardware Guide, and VARBusiness Magazine covering a variety of technology beats and trends.

Prior to becoming a technology journalist in 2000, he worked as a weekly and daily newspaper reporter in Virginia, where he won three Virginia Press Association awards in 1998 and 1999. At TechTarget and Dark Reading, he has won several Azbee awards, including the 2026 National Silver Award for a series on vibe coding.

At Dark Reading, Rob currently covers security operations, cloud security, and Internet infrastructure. He has a keen interest in malvertising activity and the certificate authority industry, and has written extensively on both topics. He graduated from the University of Richmond in 1997 with a degree in journalism and English. A native of Massachusetts, he lives in the Boston area.

#9736. Salesforce Pays $5.66B for Braze, Buying the Rival That Outran Marketing Cloud

Diverse entities united, strength in diversity, harnessing synergies for innovative growth and resilience.

Diverse entities united, strength in diversity, harnessing synergies for innovative growth and resilience.

Diverse entities united, strength in diversity, harnessing synergies for innovative growth and resilience.

On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire Braze, the New York customer engagement platform, for about $5.66 billion in enterprise value. Braze Class A holders get $47.50 in cash per share, a roughly 58% premium to the prior close of $30.04. The deal is expected to close in Salesforce's fiscal 2028, pending Braze shareholder and regulatory approval, with "no anticipated change to Salesforce's FY27 guidance."

This is no sleepy tuck-in. Salesforce is buying the real-time, event-driven engagement layer that Marketing Cloud has long been accused of lacking, and removing a competitor that was winning brands that outgrew or fled its ecosystem. The market reaction captured the tension: Braze rose 51% and Salesforce fell 3% as investors weighed the cash against the logic.

Marketing Cloud has been a soft spot. Specialized rivals and the rise of mobile-first, high-volume consumer apps left Salesforce playing catch-up, and Braze was built for exactly that world. Salesforce itself describes Braze as "optimized for high-volume, real-time B2C engagement."

"Every interaction is an opportunity to wow your customers," said Patrick Stokes, Salesforce's President of Applications and Marketing. "Braze was built to turn live customer behavior into personalized engagement at scale." The plan is to fold Braze's real-time engine and AI decisioning into all four layers of Salesforce's architecture: Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce and SIForce.

The deal fits a pattern. Salesforce bought Fin, formerly Intercom, for about $3.6 billion earlier in 2026 to bolster agentic customer service, and closed its roughly $8 billion Informatica deal in 2025 for data. Reuters framed Braze as "the latest bet by Salesforce to accelerate its AI transition" as investors worry AI could erode demand for traditional software. Both companies tout an "open, composable approach" that should ease integration in theory. Salesforce's integration history, from Slack onward, suggests theory and practice do not always align.

At $47.50, Salesforce is paying just over six times Braze's projected annual sales. Evercore ISI's Kirk Materne said the size of the premium "seems a bit odd unless it was competitive", while granting that "the deal logic makes sense." Piper Sandler's Billy Fitzsimmons downgraded Braze to Neutral, lifted his target to $47.50, and framed the deal as Salesforce removing a growing competitor to Marketing Cloud.

The downgrades piled up as analysts moved to the deal price: BTIG, Piper Sandler, Wells Fargo and Oppenheimer all cut ratings, and Loop Capital followed. Jefferies argued the acquisition "re-energizes Marketing & Commerce Cloud". Rival Klaviyo jumped more than 12% as the market priced in either more consolidation or validation of the category.

Braze serves about 2,770 customers, including Canva, Dairy Queen, Equinox, Instacart, Urban Outfitters and Venmo. For years, a core Braze sales motion was positioning itself as the modern alternative to Marketing Cloud: real-time, mobile-native, lighter. RepVue's Adam Little noted that Braze reps ranked Salesforce as one of the competitors they faced most often in head-to-head deals. Customers who chose Braze to escape the Salesforce orbit now face being pulled back in.

Longtime Marketing Cloud users may read the deal as Salesforce conceding that its own platform never fully adapted to the real-time, mobile-first era. Markup AI's Holly Enneking put the open question this way: "whether Salesforce can preserve the focus that made Braze competitive."

Executive statements, analyst notes and reactions from the press and X, grouped by theme.

"Most of that wow comes from knowing your customer, and responding at just the right moment." — Patrick Stokes, Salesforce

"Braze was built on the conviction that marketers and their creativity are a brand's ultimate competitive advantage." — Bill Magnuson, CEO and co-founder, Braze

"We'll continue building as Braze." — Bill Magnuson, via CMSWire

"The extent of that premium seems a bit odd unless it was competitive." — Kirk Materne, Evercore ISI, via MarketWatch

Salesforce is buying "a real-time engagement layer that its marketing business has historically lacked." — Shay Boloor, Futurum Equities, via Reuters

The deal "re-energizes Marketing & Commerce Cloud." — Jefferies, via Business Insider

The technology stacks at Salesforce and Adobe remain core to enterprise marketing, but their ability to compete has diminished "to the point where M&A was and remains a necessity." — Rob Oliver, Baird, via MarketWatch

"That shows how much real-time customer engagement matters to brands right now." — Jeremy Swift, CEO, Cordial

"Most of the work marketers do will happen through agents, in conversation." — Pini Yakuel, CEO, Optimove

The deal "feels like Salesforce buying both the next chapter and one of the strongest challengers to its existing business." — Holly Enneking, Markup AI

"Existing Braze customers, who signed up on the promise of a better Salesforce, are now tied to the very ecosystem they worked so hard to leave behind." — Simon Dawlat

"Braze was selling hard against Salesforce and doing a good job at it. If you can't beat em, buy em." — Adam Little, RepVue

"Specialist software names have underperformed in an AI infrastructure-driven market. Braze is a textbook example." — Jon Fortt

"Strategic fit isn't the same as shareholder value. Can AI-driven growth justify the premium, or is Salesforce overpaying?" — Patch

"A buyer who signs a two-year runway and guides to nothing on the other side is not buying next year's revenue." — Thomas Smale

A fiscal 2028 close gives both companies time, and gives competitors time to respond. Integration is the real test. The open, composable architecture is a good sign, but cultural fit, product roadmaps and keeping Braze's engineers will matter more than press-release language about "wow."

For the wider software market, the deal adds a data point to the AI consolidation thesis: specialized platforms that own a critical workflow layer stay valuable even when public multiples compress. Salesforce's stock slide also shows investors no longer write blank checks for AI-adjacent purchases. The premium has to show up in growth, margins or both.

Braze customers will watch for signals on product independence, pricing and roadmap continuity. Marketing Cloud customers will watch to see whether Braze's technology lands in the product they use daily. And the rest of the MarTech landscape will recalibrate: if the "better Salesforce" can be bought, the incentives for the next generation of engagement platforms just changed.

The deal is logical. Whether it is wise will show up in the product that ships two years from now, not in today's stock chart.

#9735. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9734. ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests

A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.

The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing.

On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.

Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.

Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.

In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.

Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.

In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.

“We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.”

A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.”

Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines, which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed.

However, as noted in our November 2025 profile of Rey, his family’s shared computer was at one point compromised by password-stealing malware, and the data collected by that malware clearly shows Rey’s father used the same credentials to log in at multiple online portals for Royal Jordanian Airlines employees.

Royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims.

Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it shows that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p.

Rey’s blog on GitHub. This post doxes two Russian men as the core operators behind Cl0p, one of the oldest and most established ransomware groups still in operation today.

Meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. The Dutch daily RTL reported on Sept. 29 that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. According to RTL, the murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for these attacks.

Van der Stap was released from prison after serving the better part of a four year sentence for data theft and extortion activity that prosecutors said netted between €1.5 million and €2.7 million. In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, Van der Stap described his new role as “offensive security lead” at the Dutch cybersecurity company Neo Security, saying the job involved probing client networks for security vulnerabilities.

Neo Security’s owner Benjamin Korper told Reuters he has hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but that so far investigators have found no evidence he acted against his employer or clients. Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office on September 15, the night Van der ⁠Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that reportedly involved flash bang grenades.

A screenshot of a Sept 16 story by the Dutch news outlet at5.nl, describing a police raid on Van Der Stap’s residence that reportedly used flash-bang grenades.

Prior to his first arrest in 2023, Van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) — even as he was hacking into and extorting a number of large organizations.

When asked in a recent interview why anyone should believe the word of a self-described “reformed” cybercriminal who had so casually deceived countless friends, co-workers and journalists for years, Van der Stap replied that his work spoke for itself and there was nothing he could say that would convince his worst critics.

“You can throw a bunch of nice words at someone, but you can’t convince them if they don’t want to be convinced,” Van der Stap told KrebsOnSecurity on Sept. 9. “I’m doing what I can to repay victims, and that’s all I can do. If someone doesn’t want to believe me, then that’s on them.”

Cybercriminals aligned with ShinyHunters have been responsible for dozens of data breaches involving billions of stolen records, and breaches claimed by the group stretch back to at least 2019. But experts say the people recently operating behind the ShinyHunters name are not the same core members that populated the group in its early days, most of whom are French citizens who have been arrested (if not also imprisoned) on at least one prior occasion for alleged cybercrime activity.

More to the point, ShinyHunters has become something of a franchise. Think the Dread Pirate Roberts character in the 1980s cult movie classic “The Princess Bride,” only succession by death is replaced with succession by arrest, and there can be multiple simultaneous Dread Pirate Robertses. Sources close to the investigation say the FBI is focusing on a remaining handful of cybercriminal freelancers or affiliates who have been feeding the group stolen credentials to various software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms used by major companies in exchange for a cut of any data ransoms later paid by victims.

In the days after the news broke of Van der Stap’s arrest, a cybercrime-focused chat server on Telegram that was allegedly operated by Rey erupted with hot takes, with most participants heaping ridicule on the teenage hacker after he publicly backed down from threats against the FBI and Cl0p, and again when the ShinyHunters’s darknet website suddenly went offline. Several commentators accused Rey of resurrecting the ShinyHunters brand after its core members were rounded up in France, and making a mockery of the group’s name and reputation ever since.

“He bought the old forum PGP key and used it to make new Breachforum websites and Telegram channels larping as ShinyHunters to ransom companies and then sell the used data or resell his forum when he goes broke,” one member recounted.

A relatively new Telegram channel called “The Battle” has been doxing and needling Rey and other alleged ShinyHunters members for several weeks, and it has gained a considerable readership among the cybercrime communities operating on Telegram. One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.

“Rey (Saif Al-Din Khader) made a serious mistake when he started pretending to be a member of ShinyHunters,” wrote the administrators of The Battle server on Telegram. “That group had already been dismantled, with many of its members either arrested or imprisoned, yet Rey still chose to use its name while carrying out his crimes. We’re aware of claims that [Rey] caused over $200 million in damages and helped around 5–6 friend groups in the community make money by using Shiny Hunters group aliases to negotiate deals for a 25–30% cut over the past few months.”

In an interview with The Register, ShinyHunters claimed they hacked the FBI to counter the agency’s narrative in a May 2026 alert that advised victims against paying a ransom to the group, which came off looking unprofessional and capricious in the FBI’s advisory.

A flash notice on ShinyHunters released by the FBI on May 15, 2026.

The public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims. The FBI warned ShinyHunters members “may also falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

The hackers told The Register their attack on the FBI “demonstrated our technical capabilities and directly refuted the misinformation disseminated by the FBI, journalists, and industry researchers.” At the same time, the group’s leaders seemed to acknowledge that the FBI’s warning materially harmed their prospects for convincing victims to pay, saying “this was fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.”

#9733. NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

New guidance provides a basic framework for less-technical solo business owners, but it may miss the mark on how to secure technology that requires no human oversight.

Threat actors always target the path of least resistance, and for years that's been small-to-medium sized businesses (SMBs). Now, new guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) aims to help companies with possibly even fewer resources: "solopreneurs."

For solo business owners, incidents can be a dealbreaker, with some shuttering completely following an attack. But risks also extend through the supply chain, as threat actors exploit vulnerabilities as a backdoor to hit larger enterprises.

NIST has published the Cybersecurity White Paper 50 (CSWP), a series of recommendations on how to curb cyber risks for a population that makes up 81.9% of all U.S. businesses.

The agency is trying to offset challenges with guidance for password hygiene, ransomware threats, and adhering to regulations requirements— areas where solopreneurs typically lack the time, money, or people to build out a security program on their own.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

NIST said the guide translates its Cybersecurity Framework into lay language for non-employer firms. But with 33 pages to work through, is it worth the investment?

Most of the practical core is within reach for solopreneurs, says Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender. People just need to scroll to the short list on Page Two which calls for phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), a password manager, a standard (non-admin) account for daily work, automatic updates, and tested backups with one copy kept offline.

"None of that needs a security background, and you can do it in an afternoon," Zugec tells Dark Reading.

Compared to other NIST technical publications, Zugec says the CSWP is much easier to digest. Like NIST advertised, the language is plain and every action comes with a reason, a first step, and a note on what changes as businesses grow, he adds.

NIST outlined how businesses can respond to growing contractual agreements and an increasing number of suppliers and third parties as they expand operations and it becomes even more crucial to know third-parties’ cyber postures. That means staying current with regulations and establishing a formal process to manage risks that relationships could introduce.

While Bryson Byrd, cybersecurity advisor at Huntress, applauded NIST for the guidance, he says it still reads like it was written for practitioners. Terms like “least privilege,” “risk register,” and “data sensitivity classification” aren't the language of someone running a bakery or a consulting practice, he adds.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"For too long, solopreneurs have been an afterthought in cybersecurity guidance," Byrd tells Dark Reading. "The intent is right, but the closer guidance like this gets to the language of everyday business owners, the more likely it is to actually get implemented."

But it's not just the language, Byrd says. It also assumes the owner knows how to turn on logging, review account sessions, and work though a separate spreadsheet of worksheets. And he points to a recommendation on obtaining legal counsel's input before notifying customers following an incident as an extra cost that often is not in the budget.

The guidance doesn’t appear to take into consideration that "nobody goes into business to build the most secure company that exists," he adds, but to build something over time. Every hour a solopreneur spends on asset inventories, backup testing, tabletop exercises, and compliance tracking is an hour taken away from running the business, which is the priority.

"Asking a single person to do all of this is extraordinarily cumbersome and, quite frankly, unrealistic," Byrd explains.

Byrd observes gaps in the guidance in places "we see hurt small businesses in the real world." The first is domain registrar, which is important to address, since attackers regularly go after small business domains to launch impersonation attacks and siphon money from customers and partners. Control of the domain means threat actors assume control over email and the business's website too.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

"Locking down the registrar account with multi-factor authentication, enabling registrar lock, and turning on auto-renewal should be part of any baseline for a solopreneur," Byrd recommends.

The second gap he addresses is email authentication. The three core protocols — Sender Policy Framework, DomainKeys Identified Mail, and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance — are becoming more important to protect a business from being impersonated and to ensure its legitimate email is delivered, adds Byrd.

The third and perhaps most impactful for a business of one is what happens when the owner is unavailable for an extended period of time due to an illness, family matter, or simply to take a well-deserved vacation.

Ransomware groups target businesses during off-hours, weekends, and holidays. If something does happen that demands an immediate response, it's essential for someone to be there. It could mean the difference between an incident and a breach.

"A break-glass plan that gives a trusted person or partner emergency access to critical accounts is still needed, and it belongs in any cybersecurity plan for a solopreneur," he advises.

Previously, SMBs and self-employers adopted the mindset that they were too small to be considered a target. That has since been disproven tenfold and is only growing worse.

Advancements in autonomous tools and artificial intelligence (AI) have lowered the barrier to entry and the cost of attacks, letting threat actors target that population at scale. They realized they had a choice: go after large enterprises with strong defenses for one big payout, or target thousands of small shops with weak security that are far more likely to pay up.

As the struggles evolved, so must the guidance. Daniel Eliot, lead for small business engagement at NIST, says this paper comes nearly 10 years after its predecessor, NISTIR 7621 rev.1.

A lot has changed in 10 years and after the initial call for comments, "that feedback was instrumental in moving the project forward."

AI is forcing a lot of security guidance to be updated and making that guidance easier to write, Zugec notes. He noticed new additions in CSWP included a section on AI and a warning that AI makes phishing more convincing.

NIST urged businesses to take a second or third look at any message that asks people to click a link, download a file, transfer funds, or log into an account.

But contrary to popular belief, AI hasn't brought any new or novel attacks, observes Zugec. It is changing who runs businesses and what they rely on to operate.

Solopreneurs are using AI assistants to read their mailboxes, run commands, write code, and use accounts under the owner's identity, he explains. While it enables one person to do the work of a small team, it also expands the attack surface.

"Many solopreneurs will use agentic AI to grow faster than their security does," he says. "The guide gives no advice on what these agents should be allowed to reach, or on securing the code they write."

The biggest gap Zugec found in the guide is "AI that acts." NIST treats AI as something passive that businesses need to inventory and review outputs for, but agentic AI has increasingly removed humans from the equation.

As agentic AI enables more people to run a business alone, the security of those businesses matters more than ever, Zugec warns. That will warrant outside help, as people increasingly turn to vibe coding to build applications on their own. He urges solopreneurs to have their code reviewed by someone with coding and security experience before anything ships.

If anything is public-facing, that means an attacker can reach it and it needs to be protected.

"AI is good at producing software that works, but not necessarily software with a small attack surface," he says. "The guide doesn't cover this, yet it's often the first risk solopreneurs run into."

Zugec spotted other weaknesses too. For example, NIST pushed for continuous updates, but a solopreneur can’t realistically track every legal and contractual security requirement, negotiate security terms with a cloud provider, or monitor their systems around the clock.

Secondly, it never ranks tasks, which makes prioritization difficult for a one-person team. For example, it opens with governance, the least actionable task, while MFA and backup advice only starts on Page 14. It also fails to cover two common attack routes: ClickFix, which tricks people into pasting a command themselves, and a malware that steals their logged-in session, which bypasses MF

"It lists around 25 actions and says outright that it isn't a checklist, so a busy owner has to decide what comes first," Zugec says. The guide also sets its scope by headcount, which is problematic. Technically the headcount would be one, but risk follows what information businesses hold and who targets them.

It's not just about size, it's about what's exposed. Risk heavily varies between someone who sells candles on Etsy as a side gig versus someone in the finance industry trading billions in cryptocurrency.

"A solo crypto operator or a consultant with client secrets needs far more than the guide’s baseline," Zugec says.

Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9732. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.

That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.

The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.

We’ve been writing about the ransomware-as-a-service supply chain here, including recent coverage of negotiation-related arrests and the FBI’s warnings to other groups.

https://cyber.murati.net/posts/shinyhunters-leader-arrested-fbi-warns-others

The irony Stalyn noted is real, but the line Dubrovsky drew in his book is genuinely important for incident response work. Communicating with the threat actor to de-escalate or buy time during containment is a different thing from facilitating a payment, and IR teams live on that distinction every day. What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Get your outside counsel involved in the ransomware response plan before you need it, not after the FBI shows up with questions about who said what on your behalf.

Well, Van der Stap also worked in the industry, doing offensive security while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerable Disclosure, and it’s well-established that ShinyHunters actively sought to recruit insiders employed at key targets, particularly telecom providers (…while making it very clear they don’t target companies in Russia, Belarus, North Korea, and China… but sure, they are “purely financially motivated”).

Fully expecting that as the FBI and European authorities dig deeper, quite a few more people will be found actively playing both sides of the fence.

The line between ‘mediating’ an extortion attempt and actively facilitating a federal crime has always been razor-thin in this industry. If negotiators are taking a cut of the payout or coordinating directly with groups like ShinyHunters beyond strict incident response, it’s no longer advisory—it’s collusion. Expect cyber insurance carriers to drastically overhaul their IR vendor requirements after this.

There is an additional important question about the whole FBI leak affair that needs to be answered: Who in the FBI moved these sensitive personnel files to a server that could be penetrated by outsiders? My guess is that somebody in DOGE did it, in preparation for downloading the files to the DOGE network outside the FBI. This might also mean that private parties in the U.S. have had these files for a long time.

Perhaps the next administration will want to get to the bottom of this and punish the perpetrators, if any. The Trump administration most certainly will not.

The breached application is Oracle PeopleSoft — specifically, an unpatched vulnerability in its Environment Management Hub platform tracked as CVE-2026-35273. According to reports last week, the FBI removed an Accenture contractor that was responsible for keeping it updated.

Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is visibility into what the group actually does to get in.

Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:

– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect, Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability. – Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early. – Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one transfer to be useful to the extortion side.

The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.

We covered the detection angle in more depth here: https://cyber.murati.net/posts/fbi-tells-shinyhunters-members-to-turn-themselves-in-after-recent-arrest

The detail about the arrest happening while he was in town for the Cyber Risk Summit at the Loews is wild, feels like it was ripped from a thriller. I get that ransomware response is high stakes, but a negotiation firm being linked to the group it’s supposed to be fighting is a huge trust problem. For stuff like cleaning up product images at scale I just use a bulk background remover and move on, but clearly cybercrime is a whole different mess.

This is the normal ‘orange’ RaaS business. And it’s a now legitimate SaaS. **Securiry Lab LLC** should trip to tax havens. A sycophantic chatbot investigates the Epstein files. What a terrible joke.

Not sure why this is being mentioned like something abnormal: “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”.

Any reputable IR firm does exactly that. It is so valuable, that threat actors start denying access to some information. I lost the count of cases where clients felt more relief after we start comms and decided not to pay because of that communication.

Threat actors are intentionally applying pressure to force exactly the scenario you describe. Your security recommendation is to essentially play into their hands.

No reporting in this? https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-canadian-cybersecurity-executive-arrested-by-fbi-was-in-legal-battle/
